topics.summary: This topic covers base and derived quantities, SI units, dimensions, measuring instruments and how errors combine. In NSMQ it shows up as quick dimension checks, unit conversions, instrument readings and percentage-error questions, and dimensional reasoning helps rule out wrong options in every other topic too.
keyIdeas: The seven SI base quantities and units are length (m), mass (kg), time (s), electric current (A), temperature (K), amount of substance (mol) and luminous intensity (cd).
Derived quantities are built from base quantities, e.g. force in N = kg m s⁻², energy in J = kg m² s⁻², power in W = kg m² s⁻³.
Scalars have magnitude only (mass, energy, speed); vectors have magnitude and direction (displacement, velocity, force, momentum).
An equation can only be physically correct if every term has the same dimensions; a dimensionally correct equation can still be wrong by a pure number such as 2π.
Accuracy is closeness to the true value; precision is how close repeated readings are to each other and how fine the instrument scale is.
Systematic errors (such as zero error) shift every reading the same way and are not reduced by averaging; random errors scatter readings and are reduced by averaging.
Least count of a vernier caliper is usually 0.1 mm (0.01 cm); a micrometer screw gauge is usually 0.01 mm.
Prefixes go in steps of 10³: n (10⁻⁹), μ (10⁻⁶), m (10⁻³), k (10³), M (10⁶), G (10⁹).

formulas.name: Percentage error
formulas.note: Δx is the absolute uncertainty in the measured value x.

formulas.name: Errors in sums and differences
formulas.formula: Q = a ± b  ⇒  ΔQ = Δa + Δb
formulas.note: Absolute errors add, even when the quantities are subtracted.

formulas.name: Errors in products and quotients
formulas.formula: Q = ab or a/b  ⇒  ΔQ/Q = Δa/a + Δb/b
formulas.note: Fractional (or percentage) errors add for maximum error.

formulas.name: Errors in powers
formulas.note: The power multiplies the percentage error; works for roots too (n = ½).

formulas.name: Vernier caliper reading
formulas.formula: Reading = main scale reading + (coinciding vernier division × least count)
formulas.note: Least count = 1 main scale division − 1 vernier scale division, typically 0.01 cm.

formulas.name: Micrometer reading
formulas.formula: Reading = sleeve reading + (thimble division × least count); least count = pitch / number of thimble divisions
formulas.note: Pitch 0.5 mm with 50 divisions gives least count 0.01 mm.

formulas.name: Zero error correction
formulas.formula: Correct reading = observed reading − zero error
formulas.note: Zero error is positive if the instrument reads above zero when closed, negative if below.

formulas.name: Common dimensions
formulas.note: Torque has the same dimensions as energy but is not energy.

formulas.name: Density
formulas.note: SI unit kg m⁻³; 1 g cm⁻³ = 1000 kg m⁻³.

formulas.name: Speed conversion
formulas.note: Multiply m/s by 3.6 to get km/h.

shortcuts.name: km/h to m/s
shortcuts.rule: Divide by 3.6, or multiply by 5/18; multiples of 18 km/h convert cleanly (18 → 5, 36 → 10, 72 → 20, 90 → 25, 108 → 30).

shortcuts.name: Error scales with the power
shortcuts.rule: For Q ∝ aⁿ, multiply the percentage error of a by n; ignore constants like 4/3 and π.
shortcuts.example: Sphere radius measured with 2% error: V = (4/3)πr³ so V has 3 × 2% = 6% error.

shortcuts.name: Combined percentage error by inspection
shortcuts.rule: For a product or quotient of powers, multiply each percentage error by its power and add them all — division still adds.
shortcuts.example: g = 4π²L/T² with 1% error in L and 0.5% error in T: 1% + 2 × 0.5% = 2%.

shortcuts.name: Derive a formula by dimensions
shortcuts.rule: Write the quantity as a product of powers, match M, L, T exponents and solve.
shortcuts.example: Wave speed on a string v = Tᵃμᵇ (T tension, μ mass per length): [MLT⁻²]ᵃ[ML⁻¹]ᵇ = LT⁻¹ gives a + b = 0, a − b = 1, −2a = −1, so a = ½, b = −½ and v = √(T/μ).

shortcuts.name: Dimension check to eliminate options
shortcuts.rule: Check only the dimensions of each option; any option that does not reduce to the right dimensions is out.
shortcuts.example: Pendulum period options √(l/g) and √(g/l): √(L ÷ LT⁻²) = √(T²) = T, so √(l/g) is the only possible form.

shortcuts.name: Vernier reading in one line
shortcuts.rule: Main scale reading, then append the coinciding vernier division as the next digit when least count is 0.01 cm.
shortcuts.example: Main scale 2.3 cm, 7th vernier division coincides: reading = 2.3 + 7 × 0.01 = 2.37 cm.

traps: Saying the gram is the SI base unit of mass; it is the kilogram.
Subtracting errors when quantities are subtracted; absolute errors always add.
Adding a zero error instead of subtracting it (a negative zero error must be added to the reading, a positive one subtracted).
Treating a dimensionally correct equation as automatically correct; dimensions cannot detect pure numbers like ½ or 2π.
Listing speed or energy as vectors; they are scalars.
nsmqTips: When asked for the unit of a quantity in base units, write its defining formula and substitute: e.g. pressure = force/area = kg m s⁻² / m² = kg m⁻¹ s⁻².
For riddles about instruments, know which reads to 0.1 mm (vernier) and which to 0.01 mm (micrometer).
In multiple-choice formula questions, run a quick dimension check first; it often leaves one option.
State units with every numerical answer; quizmasters may reject a bare number.

topics.summary: Kinematics describes motion with displacement, velocity and acceleration, using graphs and the equations of uniformly accelerated motion. Projectile questions split motion into a uniform horizontal part and a uniformly accelerated vertical part, and they are a favourite NSMQ speed round.
keyIdeas: The equations of motion apply only when acceleration is constant.
The gradient of a displacement–time graph is velocity; the gradient of a velocity–time graph is acceleration; the area under a velocity–time graph is displacement.
Free-fall acceleration g ≈ 9.8 m s⁻² (often 10 m s⁻² in quiz work) acts downward at all times, including at the top of the path.
In projectile motion (no air resistance) horizontal velocity stays constant and vertical motion has acceleration g downward; the two are independent.
At maximum height the vertical velocity is zero but the horizontal velocity u cosθ remains.
For launch and landing at the same level, range is greatest at 45°, and complementary angles (θ and 90° − θ) give the same range.
A body dropped and a body thrown horizontally from the same height reach the ground at the same time.
Relative velocity of A with respect to B is v_A − v_B (vector subtraction).

formulas.name: Velocity–time
formulas.note: u initial velocity, v final velocity, a constant acceleration, t time.

formulas.name: Displacement–time
formulas.note: Use when final velocity is not given.

formulas.name: Velocity–displacement
formulas.note: Use when time is not given.

formulas.name: Average velocity form
formulas.note: Use when acceleration is not given.

formulas.name: Distance in the nth second
formulas.note: Displacement during the nth second only, not up to it.

formulas.name: Time of flight
formulas.note: Projectile launched and landing at the same level, θ above horizontal.

formulas.name: Maximum height
formulas.note: Depends only on the vertical component u sinθ.

formulas.name: Range
formulas.formula: R = u² sin2θ / g; R_max = u²/g at θ = 45°
formulas.note: Same launch and landing height, no air resistance.

formulas.name: Trajectory equation
formulas.formula: y = x tanθ − g x² / (2u² cos²θ)
formulas.note: A parabola; y is height at horizontal distance x.

formulas.name: Horizontal launch from height h
formulas.note: u is the horizontal launch speed.

formulas.name: Vertical throw
formulas.formula: Max height = u²/(2g); time to top = u/g; total time = 2u/g
formulas.note: Thrown straight up from ground level.

shortcuts.name: Odd-number rule (Galileo)
shortcuts.rule: From rest under constant acceleration, distances covered in successive equal time intervals are in ratio 1 : 3 : 5 : 7 …
shortcuts.example: Dropped stone with g = 10 m s⁻²: 5 m in the 1st second, 15 m in the 2nd, 25 m in the 3rd; total after 3 s = 45 m.

shortcuts.name: Complementary angles
shortcuts.rule: Angles θ and 90° − θ give the same range at the same speed; only the height and flight time differ.

shortcuts.name: Range–height link
shortcuts.rule: R tanθ = 4H, so at 45° the range is four times the maximum height.
shortcuts.example: A ball at 45° reaches a maximum height of 5 m: range = 4 × 5 = 20 m.

shortcuts.name: Height from flight time
shortcuts.rule: H = gT²/8 for a symmetric flight (half the flight is a fall from the top).
shortcuts.example: Time of flight 4 s, g = 10: H = 10 × 16 / 8 = 20 m (check: falling for 2 s gives ½ × 10 × 2² = 20 m).

shortcuts.name: Stopping distance scales as speed squared
shortcuts.rule: With the same braking deceleration, stopping distance ∝ u².
shortcuts.example: A car stops in 20 m from 36 km/h; from 72 km/h (double speed) it needs 4 × 20 = 80 m.

shortcuts.name: Vertical throw in multiples of 10
shortcuts.rule: With g = 10, time to top = u/10 and height = u²/20.
shortcuts.example: u = 30 m s⁻¹: reaches top in 3 s, height = 900/20 = 45 m, lands after 6 s.

traps: Saying the acceleration at the top of a projectile path is zero; it is still g downward.
Saying the velocity at the top is zero for an angled projectile; only the vertical component is zero.
Mixing sign conventions: if up is positive, g must be −9.8 m s⁻² throughout.
Using the range formula R = u² sin2θ / g when launch and landing heights are different.
Confusing distance travelled in the nth second with total distance travelled in n seconds.
nsmqTips: Most quiz projectile problems use g = 10 m s⁻² and angles of 30°, 45°, 60°; memorise sin30° = 0.5, sin45° ≈ 0.707, sin60° ≈ 0.866.
For graph questions, say immediately what the gradient and the area represent; that usually is the answer.
In 'which reaches the ground first' riddles, only the vertical motion matters.
Write down the three known quantities among u, v, a, s, t and pick the equation without the missing one.

topics.summary: Newton's three laws relate force to changes in motion, and momentum conservation follows from the third law. NSMQ uses this topic for lift problems, connected bodies, recoil and collision calculations where knowing the standard results saves a lot of time.
keyIdeas: First law: a body stays at rest or in uniform straight-line motion unless a resultant external force acts; inertia is measured by mass.
Second law: resultant force equals rate of change of momentum, F = Δp/Δt, which reduces to F = ma for constant mass.
Third law: forces come in equal and opposite pairs acting on different bodies, so they never cancel each other on one body.
Impulse FΔt equals change in momentum; it is the area under a force–time graph.
Total momentum of an isolated system is conserved in all collisions and explosions.
Kinetic energy is conserved only in elastic collisions; in inelastic collisions some becomes heat, sound or deformation.
Coefficient of restitution e = 1 for perfectly elastic, 0 for perfectly inelastic (bodies stick together), between 0 and 1 otherwise.
Weight is a force (W = mg, in newtons); mass is the amount of matter (kg) and is the same everywhere.

formulas.name: Newton's second law
formulas.note: F is the resultant force on the body.

formulas.name: Momentum
formulas.note: Vector; unit kg m s⁻¹ or N s.

formulas.name: Impulse
formulas.note: For a ball bouncing back, Δp = m(v + u) when speeds are taken as magnitudes.

formulas.name: Conservation of momentum
formulas.note: Take one direction as positive; velocities in the other direction are negative.

formulas.name: Coefficient of restitution
formulas.note: Relative speed of separation divided by relative speed of approach.

formulas.name: Perfectly inelastic collision
formulas.note: Bodies move off together.

formulas.name: Elastic collision, target at rest
formulas.note: One-dimensional, m₂ initially at rest.

formulas.name: Kinetic energy and momentum
formulas.note: For equal momenta, KE ∝ 1/m.

formulas.name: Apparent weight in a lift
formulas.formula: R = m(g + a) going up with acceleration a; R = m(g − a) accelerating downward
formulas.note: In free fall a = g and R = 0.

formulas.name: Atwood machine
formulas.note: Two masses over a light frictionless pulley, m₁ > m₂.

formulas.name: Recoil
formulas.note: Total momentum is zero before firing, so it is zero after.

shortcuts.name: Equal masses swap velocities
shortcuts.rule: In a 1D elastic collision between equal masses, the velocities are exchanged.
shortcuts.example: A 0.2 kg ball at 5 m s⁻¹ hits an identical ball at rest elastically: the first stops, the second moves at 5 m s⁻¹.

shortcuts.name: Fraction of KE lost when sticking to a body at rest
shortcuts.rule: Fraction lost = m₂/(m₁ + m₂), where m₂ is the target at rest.
shortcuts.example: 2 kg at 6 m s⁻¹ hits 4 kg at rest and sticks: fraction lost = 4/6 = 2/3. Check: KE before 36 J, v = 12/6 = 2 m s⁻¹, KE after ½ × 6 × 4 = 12 J, lost 24 J = 2/3.

shortcuts.name: Recoil energy ratio
shortcuts.rule: In an explosion from rest, the two parts have equal momenta, so their KE ratio is the inverse of their mass ratio.
shortcuts.example: 0.01 kg bullet at 400 m s⁻¹ from a 4 kg gun: p = 4 N s, gun speed 1 m s⁻¹, gun KE 2 J, bullet KE 800 J (ratio 400 = 4/0.01).

shortcuts.name: Atwood in fractions of g
shortcuts.rule: a = g × (difference / sum) of the masses.

shortcuts.name: Lift reading in one step
shortcuts.rule: Replace g by (g + a) for upward acceleration or (g − a) for downward acceleration; constant velocity means normal weight.
shortcuts.example: 60 kg person, lift accelerating up at 2 m s⁻², g = 10: scale reads 60 × 12 = 720 N; with the cable cut it reads 0.

shortcuts.name: Limiting cases of elastic collision
shortcuts.rule: Heavy hits light at rest: light moves off at about 2u. Light hits very heavy wall: bounces back with the same speed.
shortcuts.example: A truck at 10 m s⁻¹ hits a tennis ball at rest elastically: the ball leaves at about 20 m s⁻¹.

traps: Claiming action and reaction cancel; they act on different bodies.
Forgetting momentum is a vector: a 0.1 kg ball hitting a wall at 10 m s⁻¹ and bouncing back at 10 m s⁻¹ has Δp = 2 N s, not 0.
Assuming kinetic energy is conserved in every collision; only momentum is always conserved.
Giving weight in kg; weight is a force measured in newtons.
Using the resultant of only some forces in F = ma; F must be the net force.
nsmqTips: Recognise the collision type from the wording: 'stick together' or 'coalesce' means perfectly inelastic; 'elastic' means KE also conserved.
For 'why does a gun recoil' or 'why do we bend our knees on landing' questions, name the law (third law, impulse) in your first sentence.
Memorise the equal-mass and target-at-rest results; they answer many questions instantly.
For F–t graphs, the area is impulse; divide by mass to get the change in velocity.

topics.summary: Work is energy transferred by a force moving through a displacement, and power is the rate of transfer. NSMQ asks about energy conservation, machines and efficiency, pumps and vehicles, and many answers come quickly from scaling and conservation arguments.
keyIdeas: Work is done only when the force has a component along the displacement; W = 0 when force is perpendicular to motion.
Energy cannot be created or destroyed, only converted; in the absence of friction, mechanical energy (KE + PE) is constant.
The work–energy theorem: net work done on a body equals its change in kinetic energy.
Power is the rate of doing work; for a vehicle at constant speed, P = Fv where F is the driving force equal to resistance.
The kilowatt-hour is a unit of energy: 1 kWh = 3.6 × 10⁶ J.
For machines: mechanical advantage MA = load/effort, velocity ratio VR = distance moved by effort / distance moved by load, efficiency = MA/VR.
No real machine has efficiency of 100% because of friction and the weight of moving parts.
The speed reached on a frictionless slope depends only on the vertical drop, not the shape of the slope.

formulas.name: Work done
formulas.note: θ is the angle between force and displacement; unit joule.

formulas.name: Kinetic energy
formulas.note: Also KE = p²/(2m).

formulas.name: Gravitational potential energy
formulas.note: Valid near the Earth's surface where g is constant.

formulas.name: Elastic potential energy
formulas.note: Spring obeying Hooke's law, extension x.

formulas.name: Work–energy theorem
formulas.note: Use for braking distances and work done by friction.

formulas.name: Power
formulas.note: Unit watt (J s⁻¹).

formulas.name: Efficiency
formulas.note: Can also use useful power out / power in.

formulas.name: Machine ratios
formulas.formula: MA = load/effort; VR = effort distance / load distance
formulas.note: Pulley system VR = number of supporting rope sections; inclined plane VR = length/height.

formulas.name: Pump power
formulas.formula: P = mgh/t (+ ½mv²/t if water leaves with speed v)
formulas.note: m/t is the mass of water lifted per second.

formulas.name: Energy unit conversion
formulas.note: Electricity bills use kWh.

shortcuts.name: Free-fall speed table
shortcuts.rule: With g = 10, falling h = 5n² metres gives v = 10n m s⁻¹.
shortcuts.example: Fall of 5 m → 10 m s⁻¹; 20 m → 20 m s⁻¹; 45 m → 30 m s⁻¹; 80 m → 40 m s⁻¹.

shortcuts.name: Percentage change in KE
shortcuts.rule: KE ∝ v² and KE ∝ p², so square the factor.
shortcuts.example: Speed up 10%: KE × 1.1² = 1.21, a 21% rise. Momentum up 20%: KE × 1.44, a 44% rise.

shortcuts.name: Power at constant speed
shortcuts.rule: At steady speed driving force equals resistance, so P = resistance × speed.
shortcuts.example: A car meets 1500 N resistance at 20 m s⁻¹: P = 1500 × 20 = 30 000 W = 30 kW.

shortcuts.name: Pump power by mental arithmetic
shortcuts.rule: Work out mgh first, then divide by the time in seconds.
shortcuts.example: Lift 600 kg of water through 10 m in 1 minute, g = 10: 600 × 10 × 10 = 60 000 J, ÷ 60 s = 1 kW.

shortcuts.name: Efficiency from MA and VR
shortcuts.rule: η = MA/VR; skip the energy calculation.
shortcuts.example: Load 400 N, effort 100 N, VR 5: MA = 4, efficiency = 4/5 = 80%.

shortcuts.name: Spring energy scaling
shortcuts.rule: Elastic energy ∝ x², so doubling the compression quadruples the stored energy.
shortcuts.example: A spring stores 3 J at 2 cm; at 4 cm it stores 12 J; at 6 cm it stores 27 J.

traps: Saying a person carrying a box along level ground does work against gravity; the weight is perpendicular to the motion.
Treating the kWh as a unit of power; it is a unit of energy.
Forgetting that friction does negative work and turns mechanical energy into heat.
Giving efficiency greater than 100% after mixing up MA and VR.
Using total mass instead of mass per second in pump power questions.
nsmqTips: Questions on a body sliding or swinging without friction are usually energy conservation: mgh = ½mv², so mass cancels.
For 'calculate the cost' riddles, convert to kWh: power in kW × hours × price per kWh.
Expect pulley questions: VR equals the number of rope sections supporting the load block.
State the energy changes in order (e.g. chemical → electrical → light + heat) when asked to describe conversions.

topics.summary: Statics is the study of bodies in equilibrium under several forces, using resolution of forces, moments and centre of gravity. Friction sets the limit of equilibrium on rough surfaces. NSMQ favours beam and metre-rule balancing, incline problems and tensions in strings.
keyIdeas: A body is in equilibrium when the resultant force is zero and the resultant moment about any point is zero.
The moment of a force is force × perpendicular distance from the pivot to the line of action of the force.
A couple is two equal, opposite, parallel forces not on the same line; it produces rotation but no translation.
The weight of a uniform body acts at its geometric centre (centre of gravity).
Stability: a body is more stable with a low centre of gravity and a wide base; it topples when the line of action of its weight falls outside its base.
Static friction adjusts up to a maximum μₛR; once sliding, kinetic friction μₖR is usually slightly smaller.
Limiting friction is roughly independent of contact area and depends on the nature of the surfaces and the normal reaction.
Three non-parallel forces in equilibrium must meet at one point and can be drawn as a closed triangle.

formulas.name: Moment of a force
formulas.note: d is the perpendicular distance from the pivot; unit N m.

formulas.name: Principle of moments
formulas.formula: Σ clockwise moments = Σ anticlockwise moments
formulas.note: Take moments about a point where an unknown force acts to eliminate it.

formulas.name: Conditions for equilibrium
formulas.note: Apply to any rigid body at rest.

formulas.name: Torque of a couple
formulas.note: d is the perpendicular separation of the two forces.

formulas.name: Limiting friction
formulas.note: R is the normal reaction; μ has no units.

formulas.name: Angle of friction (repose)
formulas.note: θ is the incline angle at which a block is just about to slide.

formulas.name: Normal reaction on an incline
formulas.note: With no other forces perpendicular to the incline.

formulas.name: Acceleration down a rough incline
formulas.note: Only if tanθ > μ; otherwise the block stays at rest.

formulas.name: Lami's theorem
formulas.note: Three concurrent forces in equilibrium; each angle is the one opposite (between the other two forces).

formulas.name: Centre of gravity
formulas.note: Use for composite bodies or systems of point masses.

formulas.name: Symmetric hanging load
formulas.note: Two equal strings, each at θ to the vertical, supporting weight W.

shortcuts.name: Metre rule mass from balance
shortcuts.rule: The rule's weight acts at the 50 cm mark; balance its moment against the hanging mass about the pivot.
shortcuts.example: Uniform metre rule balances on a pivot at 40 cm with 50 g hung at 10 cm: 50 × 30 = m × 10, so m = 150 g.

shortcuts.name: Reactions by inverse distances
shortcuts.rule: A load on a beam between two supports is shared inversely to its distances from them.
shortcuts.example: 10 m light plank on supports A and B, 600 N load 2 m from A: R_B = 600 × 2/10 = 120 N, R_A = 600 − 120 = 480 N.

shortcuts.name: Friction coefficient from tilt angle
shortcuts.rule: If the block just begins to slide at angle θ, μ = tanθ — no forces needed.
shortcuts.example: Block just slides at 30°: μ = tan30° = 1/√3 ≈ 0.58; at 45°, μ = 1.

shortcuts.name: Tension in a symmetric sling
shortcuts.rule: T = W/(2cosθ); at θ = 60° to the vertical each string carries the full weight.
shortcuts.example: 20 N picture on two strings each at 60° to the vertical: T = 20/(2 × 0.5) = 20 N.

shortcuts.name: Three equal forces at 120°
shortcuts.rule: Three equal forces separated by 120° are in equilibrium by symmetry; any two have a resultant equal and opposite to the third.
shortcuts.example: Forces of 5 N, 5 N, 5 N at 120° apart: resultant = 0, and the resultant of any two is 5 N.

traps: Using the slant distance instead of the perpendicular distance in moments.
Forgetting the weight of a non-light beam acting at its centre.
Taking the normal reaction on an incline as mg instead of mg cosθ.
Using μR as the friction force when the body is not on the point of slipping; static friction can be less than μR.
Giving μ a unit; it is a ratio of two forces.
nsmqTips: Take moments about the pivot or about an unknown force so that it drops out of the equation.
Riddles on stability often point to 'low centre of gravity and wide base' (e.g. racing cars, bus design).
For 'why is friction useful or harmful' questions, give one concrete example of each: walking and brakes versus wear in engines.
In Lami's theorem questions, check you are using the angle opposite each force.

topics.summary: This topic links motion in a circle, Newton's law of gravitation and orbits, and simple harmonic motion such as pendulums and springs. NSMQ often tests scaling with r, g and l, satellite speeds, and SHM phase relations, all of which reward quick ratio reasoning.
keyIdeas: A body moving in a circle at constant speed is accelerating towards the centre; a resultant (centripetal) force is needed, supplied by tension, gravity, friction or a normal force.
Gravitational force between point masses is attractive and follows an inverse-square law.
For a satellite, gravity provides the centripetal force; orbital speed and period depend on the orbit radius, not on the satellite's mass.
A geostationary satellite orbits above the equator with a period of 24 h (one sidereal day ≈ 23 h 56 min), moving in the same direction as the Earth's rotation.
SHM: acceleration is proportional to displacement from equilibrium and directed towards it, a = −ω²x.
In SHM speed is greatest at equilibrium; acceleration is greatest at the extremes.
The period of a simple pendulum (small amplitude) is independent of the bob's mass and amplitude; the period of a mass–spring system is independent of g.
Astronauts in orbit feel weightless because they and their craft are in free fall together, not because gravity is absent.

formulas.name: Angular speed and acceleration
formulas.note: ω in rad s⁻¹; ω = 2π/T = 2πf.

formulas.name: Centripetal force
formulas.note: The net inward force, not an extra force.

formulas.name: Newton's law of gravitation
formulas.note: G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻²; r measured between centres.

formulas.name: Surface gravity
formulas.formula: g = GM/R²; at height h, g' = g R²/(R + h)²
formulas.note: At depth d inside a uniform Earth, g' = g(1 − d/R).

formulas.name: Orbital speed and period
formulas.note: T² ∝ r³ is Kepler's third law.

formulas.name: Escape velocity
formulas.note: About 11.2 km s⁻¹ for Earth; independent of mass of the object.

formulas.name: SHM displacement
formulas.note: A amplitude, φ phase constant.

formulas.name: SHM speed and acceleration
formulas.formula: v = ω√(A² − x²); v_max = Aω; a_max = ω²A
formulas.note: a = −ω²x at every point.

formulas.name: Simple pendulum
formulas.note: Small angles (below about 10°).

formulas.name: Mass–spring system
formulas.note: Same formula for horizontal or vertical springs.

formulas.name: SHM energy
formulas.note: KE = ½mω²(A² − x²), PE = ½mω²x².

formulas.name: Vertical circle limits
formulas.note: For a mass on a string going round a complete vertical circle.

shortcuts.name: Escape is √2 times orbital
shortcuts.rule: Escape speed from a surface = √2 × the speed of a circular orbit just above that surface.
shortcuts.example: Low Earth orbit ≈ 7.9 km s⁻¹, so escape ≈ 7.9 × 1.414 ≈ 11.2 km s⁻¹.

shortcuts.name: Kepler scaling
shortcuts.rule: T ∝ r^(3/2): multiply r by 4 → T × 8; by 9 → T × 27.
shortcuts.example: A satellite with period 3 h moves to an orbit of 4 times the radius: new period = 3 × 8 = 24 h.

shortcuts.name: Seconds-pendulum rule
shortcuts.rule: T ≈ 2√l (T in s, l in m) because 2π/√9.8 ≈ 2.0; period ∝ √l.
shortcuts.example: l = 1 m → T ≈ 2 s; l = 0.25 m → T ≈ 1 s; length ×4 → period ×2.

shortcuts.name: Gravity at one Earth radius up
shortcuts.rule: Doubling the distance from Earth's centre divides g by 4; tripling divides by 9.
shortcuts.example: At height h = R: g' = 9.8/4 = 2.45 m s⁻²; at h = 2R: 9.8/9 ≈ 1.09 m s⁻².

shortcuts.name: SHM at half amplitude
shortcuts.rule: At x = A/2, speed = (√3/2)v_max and KE is ¾ of the total energy.
shortcuts.example: v_max = 4 m s⁻¹: at x = A/2, v = 4 × 0.866 ≈ 3.46 m s⁻¹; if total energy is 8 J, KE = 6 J and PE = 2 J.

shortcuts.name: Vertical circle tension gap
shortcuts.rule: For a mass whirled in a vertical circle, T_bottom − T_top = 6mg (energy conservation plus F = mv²/r).
shortcuts.example: 0.5 kg stone, g = 10: tension at the bottom exceeds that at the top by 6 × 0.5 × 10 = 30 N.

traps: Drawing centripetal force as an extra force on a free-body diagram; it is the resultant of the real forces.
Measuring r from the Earth's surface instead of from its centre.
Saying a heavier pendulum bob swings faster; mass does not affect the period.
Saying the period of a mass–spring system changes on the Moon; it does not depend on g.
Thinking escape velocity depends on the mass of the object or the launch direction (ignoring air resistance).
nsmqTips: Answer satellite comparisons with ratios: higher orbit means slower speed and longer period.
Know the phase relations: velocity leads displacement by π/2 and acceleration is in antiphase (π) with displacement.
For pendulum-clock riddles: a longer pendulum (e.g. expanded in heat) has a longer period, so the clock loses time.
For 'g on a planet' questions, use g ∝ M/R²; for the same density, g ∝ R.

topics.topic: Properties of matter, pressure and fluids
topics.summary: This topic covers elasticity, pressure in fluids, flotation and upthrust, surface tension, viscosity and fluid flow. NSMQ asks quick calculations on Young's modulus, hydraulic machines, relative density and floating, plus many 'explain why' riddles about everyday fluid behaviour.
keyIdeas: Hooke's law: extension is proportional to load up to the limit of proportionality; beyond the elastic limit the material is permanently deformed.
Pressure in a fluid at rest acts equally in all directions at a given depth and depends only on depth, density and g, not on the shape of the container.
Pascal's principle: pressure applied to an enclosed liquid is transmitted equally throughout it, which is the basis of hydraulic presses and brakes.
Archimedes' principle: the upthrust on a body in a fluid equals the weight of fluid displaced.
A floating body displaces its own weight of fluid (law of flotation).
Surface tension makes a liquid surface behave like a stretched skin; water rises in narrow glass tubes, mercury is depressed.
Viscosity is internal friction in a fluid; a sphere falling through a viscous fluid reaches terminal velocity when weight = upthrust + viscous drag.
In steady flow, a fluid speeds up where the pipe narrows, and faster-moving fluid has lower pressure (Bernoulli).

formulas.name: Hooke's law
formulas.note: k is the spring constant in N m⁻¹.

formulas.name: Stress, strain and Young's modulus
formulas.formula: Stress = F/A; strain = e/L; E = stress/strain = FL/(Ae)
formulas.note: Strain has no units; E and stress are in Pa.

formulas.name: Energy stored in a stretched wire
formulas.note: Area under the force–extension graph within the proportional region.

formulas.name: Pressure
formulas.note: 1 Pa = 1 N m⁻²; 1 atm ≈ 1.01 × 10⁵ Pa.

formulas.name: Liquid pressure
formulas.note: Gauge pressure at depth h; add atmospheric pressure for absolute pressure.

formulas.name: Upthrust (Archimedes)
formulas.note: Apparent loss in weight equals upthrust.

formulas.name: Fraction submerged when floating
formulas.note: Valid only for a freely floating body.

formulas.name: Relative density
formulas.formula: RD = ρ_substance / ρ_water = weight in air / loss of weight in water
formulas.note: No units.

formulas.name: Hydraulic press
formulas.note: Force ratio = area ratio = (diameter ratio)².

formulas.name: Continuity equation
formulas.note: Incompressible fluid in steady flow.

formulas.name: Bernoulli's equation
formulas.note: Along a streamline, non-viscous incompressible steady flow.

formulas.name: Stokes' law and terminal velocity
formulas.note: η viscosity, ρ sphere density, σ fluid density.

shortcuts.name: Floating fraction equals relative density
shortcuts.rule: A floating body has the fraction RD of its volume submerged in water (RD_body / RD_liquid in another liquid).
shortcuts.example: Wood of RD 0.6 floats with 60% submerged; ice (≈ 917 kg m⁻³) floats in fresh water with about 92% submerged.

shortcuts.name: Hydraulic gain from diameters
shortcuts.rule: Force gain = (large diameter / small diameter)².
shortcuts.example: Pistons of diameter 2 cm and 20 cm: gain = 10² = 100, so 50 N on the small piston lifts 5000 N.

shortcuts.name: 10 m of water ≈ 1 atmosphere
shortcuts.rule: ρgh = 1000 × 10 × 10 = 10⁵ Pa, so each 10 m of water adds about 1 atm.
shortcuts.example: A diver 30 m deep feels about 1 + 3 = 4 atm absolute pressure.

shortcuts.name: Relative density from two weighings
shortcuts.rule: RD = weight in air / (weight in air − weight in water).
shortcuts.example: A stone weighs 10 N in air and 6 N in water: upthrust = 4 N, RD = 10/4 = 2.5.

shortcuts.name: Extension scaling for wires
shortcuts.rule: e ∝ FL/d² for the same material; multiply the factors.
shortcuts.example: Same load, wire twice as long and half the diameter: e × 2 × 4 = 8 times the extension.

shortcuts.name: Pipe narrows, speed by area ratio
shortcuts.rule: v ∝ 1/A ∝ 1/d²: halving the diameter quadruples the speed.
shortcuts.example: Water at 2 m s⁻¹ in a 4 cm pipe flows at 2 × 4 = 8 m s⁻¹ in a 2 cm section.

traps: Thinking a wider container produces more pressure at the bottom; pressure depends on depth only.
Mixing gauge and absolute pressure: at depth h, absolute pressure = P_atm + ρgh.
Saying upthrust depends on the weight of the object; it depends on the volume of fluid displaced.
Assuming faster-flowing air has higher pressure; it has lower pressure.
Giving strain a unit; it is a ratio of lengths.
nsmqTips: For 'explain why' riddles (aircraft lift, atomiser spray, ships of steel floating), name the principle first: Bernoulli, Archimedes or flotation.
Use g = 10 and ρ_water = 1000 kg m⁻³ for quick pressure answers unless told otherwise.
Ratios answer most elasticity, hydraulic and terminal-velocity questions without full substitution.
Remember why mercury is used in barometers: high density gives a short column (about 0.76 m instead of about 10 m for water).

topics.summary: Rotational dynamics extends Newton's laws to rigid bodies turning about an axis, using torque, moment of inertia and angular momentum. In NSMQ it appears in rolling-race questions, spinning skaters and flywheel energy, where knowing standard moments of inertia and the linear–rotational analogy gives fast answers.
keyIdeas: Every linear quantity has a rotational partner: displacement s ↔ angle θ, velocity v ↔ ω, acceleration a ↔ α, mass m ↔ moment of inertia I, force F ↔ torque τ, momentum p ↔ angular momentum L.
Moment of inertia depends on the mass and on how far the mass is from the chosen axis; the same body has different I about different axes.
Angular momentum is conserved when no external torque acts, so reducing I increases ω.
For rolling without slipping, v = ωR and total KE = translational + rotational.
Objects rolling down the same incline arrive in order of increasing I/(mR²), independent of their mass and radius.
In pure rolling, static friction does no work because the contact point is momentarily at rest.
The parallel-axis theorem works for any body; the perpendicular-axis theorem applies only to flat laminae.

formulas.name: Newton's second law for rotation
formulas.note: τ resultant torque about the axis, α angular acceleration.

formulas.name: Moment of inertia
formulas.note: r is the perpendicular distance of each mass element from the axis; unit kg m².

formulas.name: Angular momentum
formulas.note: Conserved when external torque is zero: I₁ω₁ = I₂ω₂.

formulas.name: Rotational kinetic energy
formulas.note: Add ½mv² for a body that also translates.

formulas.name: Standard moments of inertia
formulas.formula: Ring MR²; disc MR²/2; solid sphere 2MR²/5; hollow sphere 2MR²/3; rod about centre ML²/12; rod about end ML²/3
formulas.note: Axes through the centre (symmetry axis for ring and disc) unless stated.

formulas.name: Parallel-axis theorem
formulas.note: d is the distance between the new axis and a parallel axis through the centre of mass.

formulas.name: Perpendicular-axis theorem
formulas.note: Flat lamina only; z axis perpendicular to the plane.

formulas.name: Rotational kinematics
formulas.formula: ω = ω₀ + αt; θ = ω₀t + ½αt²; ω² = ω₀² + 2αθ
formulas.note: Constant angular acceleration.

formulas.name: Rolling down an incline
formulas.formula: a = g sinθ / (1 + I/(mR²)); v = √(2gh / (1 + I/(mR²)))
formulas.note: Rolling without slipping from rest through height h.

formulas.name: Rotational work and power
formulas.note: θ in radians.

formulas.name: Torque
formulas.note: φ is the angle between r and F.

shortcuts.name: Rolling race order
shortcuts.rule: Smallest I/(mR²) wins: solid sphere (2/5) > solid disc or cylinder (1/2) > hollow sphere (2/3) > ring or hollow cylinder (1).
shortcuts.example: A small marble and a large bowling ball (both solid spheres) tie; either beats a hoop of any mass.

shortcuts.name: Speed of a rolling solid sphere
shortcuts.rule: For a solid sphere, v = √(10gh/7); pick h as a multiple of 7 for clean numbers.
shortcuts.example: Solid sphere rolls from rest down a drop of 7 m, g = 10: v² = 10 × 10 × 7/7 = 100, so v = 10 m s⁻¹.

shortcuts.name: Fraction of KE that is rotational
shortcuts.rule: With β = I/(mR²), rotational fraction = β/(1 + β).

shortcuts.name: Skater pulling arms in
shortcuts.rule: L fixed: ω ∝ 1/I and KE = L²/(2I) ∝ 1/I.
shortcuts.example: Moment of inertia halved from 4 to 2 kg m²: spin rate doubles and kinetic energy doubles (the extra comes from the skater's muscles).

shortcuts.name: Rod: centre to end
shortcuts.rule: Shift by L/2 with the parallel-axis theorem: ML²/12 + M(L/2)² = ML²/3.
shortcuts.example: A 3 kg rod of length 2 m: about the centre I = 3 × 4/12 = 1 kg m²; about one end I = 3 × 4/3 = 4 kg m².

shortcuts.name: Acceleration of a rolling sphere on a slope
shortcuts.rule: a = (5/7)g sinθ for a solid sphere; (2/3)g sinθ for a disc; (1/2)g sinθ for a ring.
shortcuts.example: Solid sphere on a 30° slope, g = 9.8: a = (5/7) × 9.8 × 0.5 = 3.5 m s⁻².

traps: Quoting one moment of inertia for a body without stating the axis.
Assuming kinetic energy is conserved whenever angular momentum is conserved (the skater gains KE).
Using the perpendicular-axis theorem for a solid three-dimensional body.
Forgetting the rotational KE when a body rolls, which overestimates its speed.
Using θ in degrees in rotational kinematics; use radians.
nsmqTips: Learn the standard I values as fractions of MR²: 1, 1/2, 2/5, 2/3; most rolling questions reduce to these numbers.
For 'which reaches the bottom first' riddles, answer with the I/(mR²) ranking and note that mass and radius do not matter.
Use the linear–rotational dictionary to turn a rotation question into a familiar linear one.
Spinning skater, diver tucking, collapsing star spinning faster: all are conservation of angular momentum.

topics.summary: This topic covers temperature scales, heat capacity, latent heat, thermal expansion and heat transfer by conduction, convection and radiation. NSMQ uses it for calorimetry calculations, temperature conversions, radiation laws and many everyday 'explain why' riddles.
keyIdeas: Temperature measures the average kinetic energy of particles; heat is energy transferred because of a temperature difference.
A temperature change of 1 K equals a change of 1 °C; absolute temperature T(K) = θ(°C) + 273.15.
During a change of state (melting, boiling) energy is absorbed or released as latent heat with no change in temperature.
Water has a high specific heat capacity (about 4200 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹), which is why it is a good coolant and why coastal climates are mild.
Water expands when cooled from 4 °C to 0 °C (anomalous expansion), so lakes freeze from the top and water is densest at 4 °C.
Conduction occurs mainly through solids; convection needs a fluid; radiation needs no medium and can cross a vacuum.
Dull black surfaces are good absorbers and emitters of radiation; shiny silvered surfaces are poor absorbers and emitters.
In an isolated mixture, heat lost by hot bodies equals heat gained by cold bodies.

formulas.name: Specific heat capacity
formulas.note: c in J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹; Δθ can be in K or °C.

formulas.name: Heat capacity
formulas.note: For a whole object; unit J K⁻¹.

formulas.name: Latent heat
formulas.note: Water: L_f ≈ 3.34 × 10⁵ J kg⁻¹, L_v ≈ 2.26 × 10⁶ J kg⁻¹.

formulas.name: Temperature conversions
formulas.note: Ice point 0 °C = 32 °F = 273.15 K; steam point 100 °C = 212 °F.

formulas.name: Linear expansion
formulas.note: α linear expansivity in K⁻¹.

formulas.name: Area and volume expansivity
formulas.note: For isotropic solids.

formulas.name: Thermal conduction
formulas.note: k thermal conductivity, d thickness, A cross-sectional area.

formulas.name: Stefan–Boltzmann law
formulas.note: σ = 5.67 × 10⁻⁸ W m⁻² K⁻⁴; e emissivity (1 for a black body); T in kelvin.

formulas.name: Wien's displacement law
formulas.note: Hotter bodies peak at shorter wavelengths.

formulas.name: Electrical heating
formulas.note: Assumes no heat loss.

formulas.name: Method of mixtures
formulas.note: θ is the final common temperature; include the container if its heat capacity is given.

shortcuts.name: Mixing the same liquid
shortcuts.rule: Final temperature is the mass-weighted average, since c cancels.
shortcuts.example: 2 kg of water at 80 °C mixed with 3 kg at 20 °C: (2 × 80 + 3 × 20)/5 = 220/5 = 44 °C.

shortcuts.name: −40 is the same on both scales
shortcuts.rule: −40 °C = −40 °F; use (9/5)θ + 32 for exact conversion.

shortcuts.name: Stefan scaling
shortcuts.rule: Radiated power ∝ T⁴ in kelvin: doubling T gives 16 times the power.
shortcuts.example: A body heated from 27 °C to 327 °C goes from 300 K to 600 K, so it radiates 2⁴ = 16 times as much power.

shortcuts.name: Wien in one line
shortcuts.rule: T = 2.9 × 10⁻³ / λ_max; at λ_max = 500 nm, T ≈ 5800 K.
shortcuts.example: The Sun peaks near 500 nm: T = 2.9 × 10⁻³ / (5 × 10⁻⁷) = 5800 K.

shortcuts.name: Kettle time
shortcuts.rule: t = mcΔθ / P; heating 1 kg of water by 1 °C needs 4.2 kJ.
shortcuts.example: 2 kW kettle heats 1 kg of water from 20 °C to 100 °C: 1 × 4200 × 80 = 336 000 J, ÷ 2000 W = 168 s.

shortcuts.name: Expansivity multiples
shortcuts.rule: Area change uses 2α and volume change uses 3α.
shortcuts.example: α = 1.2 × 10⁻⁵ K⁻¹ for steel: β = 2.4 × 10⁻⁵ K⁻¹, γ = 3.6 × 10⁻⁵ K⁻¹.

traps: Using °C instead of K in the Stefan–Boltzmann and Wien laws.
Saying temperature rises during melting or boiling; the energy goes into latent heat.
Confusing heat (energy, J) with temperature (K or °C).
Forgetting the heat absorbed by the container in calorimetry when its heat capacity is given.
Saying water is densest at 0 °C; it is densest at about 4 °C.
nsmqTips: For 'explain why' riddles (vacuum flask, sea breeze, black kettle bottoms, gaps in railway lines), name the heat-transfer mode or property in the first sentence.
Memorise c_water ≈ 4200 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹ and L_f ≈ 3.34 × 10⁵ J kg⁻¹; most calorimetry questions use them.
A sea breeze blows from sea to land by day because land heats faster (lower specific heat capacity); the land breeze reverses at night.
In mixture problems, set up 'heat lost = heat gained' before plugging in numbers.

topics.summary: The gas laws relate pressure, volume and temperature of a fixed mass of gas, and kinetic theory explains them using moving molecules. NSMQ asks ratio-based gas law problems, molecular speeds and diffusion rates, which can usually be done without ever using the value of R.
keyIdeas: All gas law calculations need absolute temperature in kelvin.
Boyle's law: at constant temperature, P ∝ 1/V; Charles's law: at constant pressure, V ∝ T; pressure law: at constant volume, P ∝ T.
An ideal gas obeys PV = nRT exactly; real gases behave nearly ideally at low pressure and high temperature.

Kinetic theory assumptions: many molecules in random motion, negligible molecular volume, no intermolecular forces except during collisions, perfectly elastic collisions, collision time much smaller than time between collisions.
Gas pressure is caused by molecules colliding with and changing momentum at the container walls.
The average translational kinetic energy of a molecule depends only on absolute temperature: (3/2)kT.
At absolute zero (0 K) an ideal gas would have zero average kinetic energy; real gases liquefy before reaching it.
Lighter gas molecules move faster at the same temperature and diffuse faster (Graham's law).

formulas.name: Boyle's law
formulas.note: Fixed mass at constant temperature.

formulas.name: Charles's law
formulas.note: Fixed mass at constant pressure; T in K.

formulas.name: Pressure law
formulas.note: Fixed mass at constant volume; T in K.

formulas.name: General gas equation
formulas.note: Fixed mass when all three change.

formulas.name: Ideal gas equation
formulas.note: R = 8.31 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹; k = 1.38 × 10⁻²³ J K⁻¹; N_A = 6.02 × 10²³ mol⁻¹; R = N_A k.

formulas.name: Kinetic theory pressure
formulas.note: ⟨c²⟩ is the mean square speed, m mass of one molecule.

formulas.name: Mean kinetic energy of a molecule
formulas.note: Translational KE only.

formulas.name: Root mean square speed
formulas.note: M is molar mass in kg mol⁻¹.

formulas.name: Graham's law of diffusion
formulas.note: At the same temperature and pressure.

formulas.name: Dalton's law of partial pressures
formulas.note: Non-reacting gas mixture.

formulas.name: Molar volume
formulas.formula: V_m ≈ 22.4 dm³ mol⁻¹ at 0 °C and 1 atm
formulas.note: About 24 dm³ mol⁻¹ at room temperature (≈ 20–25 °C) and 1 atm.

shortcuts.name: Ratio method, no R needed
shortcuts.rule: Only the quantity that changes matters; multiply by the ratio of the new to old kelvin temperatures (or volumes).
shortcuts.example: Gas at 27 °C and 1 atm heated to 127 °C at constant volume: P = 1 × 400/300 ≈ 1.33 atm.

shortcuts.name: rms speed scales with √T
shortcuts.rule: c_rms ∝ √T: four times the kelvin temperature doubles the speed.
shortcuts.example: Gas heated from 27 °C (300 K) to 927 °C (1200 K): T × 4, so rms speed × 2.

shortcuts.name: Graham with perfect squares
shortcuts.rule: Pick molar masses whose ratio is a perfect square.
shortcuts.example: H₂ (M = 2) versus O₂ (M = 32): rate ratio = √(32/2) = √16 = 4, so hydrogen diffuses 4 times faster.

shortcuts.name: Rising bubble with 10 m rule
shortcuts.rule: Each 10 m of water adds about 1 atm; at constant temperature, volume ∝ 1/P.
shortcuts.example: A bubble of 2 cm³ at 10 m depth (≈ 2 atm) rises to the surface (1 atm): volume ≈ 4 cm³.

shortcuts.name: Same temperature, same average KE
shortcuts.rule: Different gases at the same temperature have equal mean molecular KE; only their speeds differ, as 1/√M.
shortcuts.example: He and O₂ both at 300 K: equal mean KE; helium's rms speed is √(32/4) = √8 ≈ 2.8 times that of oxygen.

traps: Using °C in gas law ratios; 27 °C to 54 °C is not a doubling of temperature (300 K to 327 K).
Using molar mass in g mol⁻¹ instead of kg mol⁻¹ in c_rms = √(3RT/M).
Mixing STP conventions: 22.4 dm³ mol⁻¹ is for 0 °C and 1 atm; at 0 °C and 100 kPa (IUPAC) it is about 22.7 dm³ mol⁻¹.
Saying heavier molecules have more average KE at the same temperature; average KE depends only on T.
Applying gas laws when the mass of gas changes (e.g. a leaking tyre).
nsmqTips: Convert every temperature to kelvin first; this alone catches most trick questions.
Expect 'state the assumptions of the kinetic theory' or 'how does kinetic theory explain pressure' — have a crisp list ready.
When a question gives a doubling or halving, answer by ratio immediately rather than substituting into PV = nRT.
Know when real gases deviate from ideal behaviour: high pressure and low temperature.

topics.summary: Thermodynamics deals with energy transfers as heat and work, the internal energy of systems, and the limits on converting heat into work. In NSMQ it appears as first-law sign questions, P–V diagram work, heat engine and refrigerator efficiencies, and entropy changes, many of which have one-line answers once the standard ratios are known.
keyIdeas: Zeroth law: if two bodies are each in thermal equilibrium with a third, they are in equilibrium with each other; this is the basis of thermometers.
First law: energy is conserved; heat supplied to a system goes into increasing internal energy and doing external work.
The internal energy of an ideal gas depends only on its temperature, so ΔU = 0 in any isothermal process and in any complete cycle.
Work done by a gas equals the area under its P–V curve; in a cycle, net work equals the area enclosed by the loop.
Isothermal: ΔT = 0; adiabatic: Q = 0; isobaric: ΔP = 0; isochoric (isovolumetric): ΔV = 0 so W = 0.
Second law: no heat engine working in a cycle can convert all the heat it takes in into work; heat does not flow by itself from cold to hot.
No engine working between two temperatures can be more efficient than a reversible (Carnot) engine working between them.
The total entropy of an isolated system never decreases; it stays constant only for reversible processes.

formulas.name: First law
formulas.note: Q heat supplied to the gas, W work done by the gas (some books use ΔU = Q + W with W done on the gas).

formulas.name: Work at constant pressure
formulas.note: Isobaric process.

formulas.name: Isothermal work (ideal gas)
formulas.note: ΔU = 0, so Q = W.

formulas.name: Adiabatic relations
formulas.note: Reversible adiabatic process, ideal gas.

formulas.name: Adiabatic work
formulas.note: Work done by the gas; equals −ΔU.

formulas.name: Molar heat capacities
formulas.note: Monatomic: C_v = (3/2)R, γ = 5/3; diatomic (room temperature): C_v = (5/2)R, γ = 7/5.

formulas.name: Internal energy change
formulas.note: Valid for any process of an ideal gas.

formulas.name: Heat engine efficiency
formulas.note: Q_h heat taken in from the hot reservoir, Q_c heat rejected.

formulas.name: Carnot efficiency
formulas.note: Maximum possible; temperatures in kelvin.

formulas.name: Refrigerator coefficient of performance
formulas.formula: COP = Q_c/W; Carnot COP = T_c/(T_h − T_c)
formulas.note: Heat pump: COP = Q_h/W = T_h/(T_h − T_c).

formulas.name: Entropy change
formulas.note: Unit J K⁻¹; for a phase change at constant T, ΔS = mL/T.

formulas.name: Isothermal entropy change of ideal gas
formulas.note: Positive for expansion.

shortcuts.name: Carnot with kelvin fractions
shortcuts.rule: Convert to K, then η = 1 − T_c/T_h as a simple fraction.
shortcuts.example: Engine between 527 °C and 27 °C: 800 K and 300 K, η = 1 − 3/8 = 5/8 = 62.5%.

shortcuts.name: Cycle work = loop area
shortcuts.rule: Over a full cycle ΔU = 0, so net heat in = net work out = area enclosed on the P–V diagram.
shortcuts.example: Rectangular cycle with ΔP = 2 × 10⁵ Pa and ΔV = 3 × 10⁻³ m³: W = 2 × 10⁵ × 3 × 10⁻³ = 600 J.

shortcuts.name: Isobaric energy split
shortcuts.rule: For isobaric heating of an ideal gas, Q : ΔU : W = C_p : C_v : R, which is 5 : 3 : 2 for a monatomic gas and 7 : 5 : 2 for a diatomic gas.
shortcuts.example: 500 J supplied to a monatomic gas at constant pressure: ΔU = 300 J, W = 200 J.

shortcuts.name: Free expansion
shortcuts.rule: Expansion into a vacuum in an insulated container: Q = 0 and W = 0, so ΔU = 0 and an ideal gas keeps the same temperature (but entropy rises).
shortcuts.example: 1 mol of ideal gas doubles its volume into a vacuum at 300 K: final temperature 300 K, ΔS = R ln 2 ≈ 5.8 J K⁻¹.

shortcuts.name: Entropy of melting
shortcuts.rule: ΔS = mL/T with T the melting point in kelvin.
shortcuts.example: Melting 1 kg of ice at 273 K: ΔS = 3.34 × 10⁵ / 273 ≈ 1220 J K⁻¹.

shortcuts.name: Carnot fridge COP
shortcuts.rule: COP = T_c/(T_h − T_c); a small temperature gap gives a large COP.
shortcuts.example: Fridge interior at 270 K, room at 300 K: COP = 270/30 = 9.

traps: Mixing sign conventions for W (work done by the gas versus on the gas); state which you are using.
Using °C in Carnot efficiency or COP formulas.
Confusing adiabatic (no heat exchange) with isothermal (constant temperature).
Claiming a perfect engine could reach 100% efficiency; that would need T_c = 0 K.
Applying C_p − C_v = R to specific heat capacities per kilogram; it holds per mole (per kilogram it is R/M).
nsmqTips: Learn the four process names with their 'zero' quantity: isothermal ΔU = 0, adiabatic Q = 0, isochoric W = 0, cyclic ΔU = 0.
For P–V diagram questions, look for the area; it usually gives the work directly.
State the second law in either the Kelvin–Planck (no engine converts all heat to work) or Clausius (no spontaneous heat flow from cold to hot) form when asked.
Quote γ = 5/3 for monatomic and 7/5 for diatomic gases without hesitation; they come up often.

topics.summary: Waves carry energy from place to place without carrying matter, and sound is a longitudinal mechanical wave that needs a medium. NSMQ rounds use this topic heavily for quick ratio questions on pipes, strings, echoes, beats, decibels and the Doppler effect.
keyIdeas: Transverse waves vibrate perpendicular to the direction of travel (light, waves on a string); longitudinal waves vibrate parallel to it (sound), forming compressions and rarefactions.
Frequency is fixed by the source and does not change when a wave enters a new medium; speed and wavelength change together.
Sound cannot travel through a vacuum; it is fastest in solids, slower in liquids and slowest in gases.
In a gas the speed of sound is proportional to √T (T in kelvin) and does not depend on pressure at constant temperature.
Pitch depends on frequency, loudness on amplitude (intensity), and quality (timbre) on the mix of overtones.
Stationary waves form when two identical waves travel in opposite directions; node to node is λ/2 and node to adjacent antinode is λ/4.
A pipe closed at one end gives only odd harmonics (1 : 3 : 5); a pipe open at both ends and a stretched string give all harmonics (1 : 2 : 3).
Human hearing range is roughly 20 Hz to 20 kHz; below is infrasound, above is ultrasound.

formulas.name: Period
