formulas.name: Echo distance
formulas.note: t is the total time from shout to echo; the sound goes there and back.

shortcuts.name: Echo in one step
shortcuts.rule: With v = 340 m/s, distance to the wall = 170 × t (t = echo time in seconds).
shortcuts.example: Echo heard after 3 s: d = 170 × 3 = 510 m. Echo after 0.5 s: d = 85 m.

shortcuts.name: Decibel arithmetic
shortcuts.rule: Multiplying intensity by 10 adds 10 dB; multiplying by 100 adds 20 dB; doubling adds about 3 dB; doubling distance from a point source (intensity ÷ 4) subtracts about 6 dB.
shortcuts.example: One machine gives 60 dB. 100 identical machines: 60 + 20 = 80 dB. A speaker reads 80 dB at 2 m; at 4 m it reads about 74 dB.

shortcuts.name: Square-root scaling for strings and gases
shortcuts.rule: f ∝ √T on a string and v ∝ √T(kelvin) in a gas: to double the result, multiply the cause by 4.
shortcuts.example: A string gives 256 Hz at 40 N tension. At 160 N (×4) it gives 512 Hz. Sound at 273 K travels 330 m/s; at 1092 K (×4) it travels 660 m/s.

shortcuts.name: Temperature correction for sound in air
shortcuts.rule: v ≈ 331 + 0.6θ m/s, θ in °C (valid near room temperature).

shortcuts.name: Closed pipe = half-length open pipe
shortcuts.rule: A closed pipe of length L has the same fundamental as an open pipe of length 2L, and its overtones are 3f₁, 5f₁, … only.
shortcuts.example: v = 340 m/s, closed pipe L = 0.85 m: f₁ = 340/(4 × 0.85) = 340/3.4 = 100 Hz; overtones 300 Hz and 500 Hz. An open pipe of 1.7 m also has f₁ = 100 Hz, but its overtones are 200 Hz and 300 Hz.

shortcuts.name: Small-speed Doppler
shortcuts.rule: When the source speed is small compared with v, the fractional change in frequency ≈ v_s/v (up when approaching, down when receding).
shortcuts.example: f = 1000 Hz, v_s = 34 m/s towards you, v = 340 m/s: approx shift = 1000 × 34/340 = 100 Hz, so f′ ≈ 1100 Hz. Exact: 1000 × 340/306 ≈ 1111 Hz.

traps: Taking node-to-node distance as λ instead of λ/2.
Listing even harmonics (2f₁, 4f₁) for a pipe closed at one end.
Forgetting to halve the time in echo problems.
Thinking frequency changes when sound passes from air into water; it is speed and wavelength that change.
Using °C instead of kelvin in v ∝ √T.
nsmqTips: Most questions are ratios: write the proportionality (f ∝ √T, f ∝ 1/L, I ∝ 1/r²) and scale, rather than plugging full formulas.
For riddles, sound clues include 'longitudinal', 'needs a medium', 'compressions and rarefactions' and 'reverberation'.
For pipes, say first whether the pipe is open or closed; that one decision fixes the whole harmonic series.
Quote I₀ = 10⁻¹² W m⁻² and the 20 Hz to 20 kHz hearing range from memory; they come up as quick recall questions.

topics.summary: Optics covers reflection, refraction, lenses, mirrors, dispersion and the wave behaviour of light (interference and diffraction). In NSMQ it gives fast numerical questions on the lens formula, refractive index, critical angle and images in mirrors.
keyIdeas: Laws of reflection: the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection, and the incident ray, reflected ray and normal lie in one plane.
A plane mirror forms a virtual, upright, laterally inverted image as far behind the mirror as the object is in front.
Light bends towards the normal on entering a denser medium; frequency stays the same while speed and wavelength decrease.
Total internal reflection needs light going from a denser to a less dense medium at an angle greater than the critical angle (used in optical fibres and prism periscopes).
A convex (converging) lens can form real or virtual images; a concave (diverging) lens and a convex mirror always form virtual, upright, diminished images.
Myopia (short sight) is corrected with a diverging lens; hypermetropia (long sight) with a converging lens.
In a prism, violet light is deviated most and red least, because the refractive index is larger for shorter wavelengths.
Interference and diffraction are evidence that light behaves as a wave; polarisation shows that it is transverse.

formulas.name: Lens and mirror formula
formulas.note: Real-is-positive convention: real distances positive, virtual negative. f positive for converging lens and concave mirror.

formulas.name: Linear magnification
formulas.note: Ratio of image distance to object distance, or image height to object height.

formulas.name: Focal length of a curved mirror
formulas.note: r radius of curvature.

formulas.name: Snell's law
formulas.formula: n₁ sin θ₁ = n₂ sin θ₂
formulas.note: θ measured from the normal. From air: n = sin i / sin r.

formulas.name: Refractive index
formulas.formula: n = c/v = real depth / apparent depth
formulas.note: c = 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s. Apparent depth formula holds for viewing from nearly overhead.

formulas.name: Critical angle
formulas.note: For the medium–air boundary. For two media: sin C = n₂/n₁ with n₁ > n₂.

formulas.name: Lateral displacement by a glass block (apparent shift)
formulas.note: t real thickness; the apparent rise of an object seen through the block.

formulas.name: Power of a lens
formulas.note: f in metres, P in dioptres (D). Converging positive, diverging negative.

formulas.name: Lenses in contact
formulas.note: Thin lenses touching each other.

formulas.name: Images between two plane mirrors
formulas.note: θ angle between mirrors; exact when 360°/θ is an even whole number.

formulas.name: Prism at minimum deviation
formulas.note: A refracting angle, D angle of minimum deviation.

formulas.name: Young's double slit fringe spacing
formulas.note: D slit-to-screen distance, d slit separation. Grating: d sin θ = nλ.

shortcuts.name: Object at 2F
shortcuts.rule: When u = 2f, then v = 2f and m = 1 (real, inverted, same size). The smallest object-to-real-image distance for a converging lens is 4f.
shortcuts.example: f = 10 cm, object at 20 cm: image at 20 cm, same size. Object and screen 40 cm apart: only one sharp position, lens in the middle.

shortcuts.name: Product over sum
shortcuts.rule: f = uv/(u + v) and v = uf/(u − f): no fractions needed.

shortcuts.name: Apparent depth
shortcuts.rule: Divide real depth by n: water (n = 4/3) looks 3/4 as deep, glass (n = 1.5) looks 2/3 as thick.
shortcuts.example: A pool 2 m deep looks 1.5 m deep. A 6 cm glass block looks 4 cm thick, so the mark rises by 2 cm.

shortcuts.name: Critical angles to memorise
shortcuts.example: Glass with n = 1.5: a ray hitting the glass–air surface at 45° inside the glass exceeds 41.8°, so it is totally internally reflected (this is how a 45° prism periscope works).

shortcuts.name: Mirror tricks
shortcuts.rule: Rotate a mirror by θ and the reflected ray turns 2θ. Walk towards a plane mirror at speed v and your image approaches you at 2v. To see your full height you need a mirror half your height.
shortcuts.example: Mirror turned 15°: reflected ray turns 30°. A student 1.8 m tall needs a mirror 0.9 m long.

shortcuts.name: Images between mirrors
shortcuts.rule: Use 360/θ − 1 for the angles NSMQ gives.
shortcuts.example: 90° → 3 images, 60° → 5, 45° → 7, 30° → 11, parallel mirrors → infinitely many.

traps: Using f in centimetres for lens power: f = 25 cm gives P = 1/0.25 = +4 D, not 0.04 D.
Mixing sign conventions halfway through a problem; choose real-is-positive or Cartesian and stick to it.
Saying red light is deviated most by a prism; violet is.
Claiming total internal reflection can happen when light goes from air into glass.
Swapping the corrections: short sight uses a concave (diverging) lens.
nsmqTips: Quickly sketch where the object is relative to F and 2F; the image type (real or virtual, bigger or smaller) usually follows without calculation.
Learn n for water (1.33) and crown glass (1.5) and the matching critical angles; they appear as quick-fire questions.
Riddles about optical fibres, mirages, sparkling diamonds or rainbows point to total internal reflection or dispersion.
Give the unit with lens power: dioptre (D), equal to m⁻¹.

topics.strand: Electric Field, Magnetic Field and Electronics
topics.summary: Electrostatics studies charges at rest, the forces and fields they produce and electric potential, and capacitors store charge and energy in an electric field. NSMQ uses it for scaling questions on Coulomb's law and quick network questions on capacitors in series and parallel.
keyIdeas: Like charges repel and unlike charges attract; charge is conserved and quantised in units of e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C.
Electric field is a vector (force per unit positive charge); potential is a scalar (work per unit charge), so potentials add algebraically.
Field lines leave positive charges, enter negative charges, never cross, and meet a conductor surface at right angles.
Inside a charged conductor at equilibrium the field is zero and the potential is constant; charge sits on the outer surface and gathers at sharp points (lightning conductors).
Capacitors in parallel have the same p.d. and their capacitances add; capacitors in series carry the same charge and their reciprocals add.
Inserting a dielectric increases capacitance by the factor εᵣ.
When a battery charges a capacitor, half of the energy it supplies (QV) is stored and half is lost as heat in the circuit.

formulas.name: Coulomb's law
formulas.formula: F = kq₁q₂/r², k = 1/(4πε₀) ≈ 9.0 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻²
formulas.note: ε₀ = 8.85 × 10⁻¹² F/m. In a medium divide by εᵣ.

formulas.name: Electric field strength
formulas.note: Units N/C or V/m.

formulas.name: Field of a point charge
formulas.note: Directed away from a positive charge.

formulas.name: Potential of a point charge
formulas.note: Scalar; sign follows the charge.

formulas.name: Uniform field between plates
formulas.note: V p.d. between plates, d separation.

formulas.name: Work done moving a charge
formulas.note: 1 eV = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ J is the energy gained by an electron across 1 V.

formulas.name: Capacitance
formulas.note: Unit farad (F); 1 μF = 10⁻⁶ F, 1 pF = 10⁻¹² F.

formulas.name: Parallel-plate capacitor
formulas.note: A plate overlap area (m²), d separation (m).

formulas.name: Energy stored
formulas.note: Choose the form that holds the constant quantity fixed.

formulas.name: Series and parallel
formulas.note: Opposite of the resistor rules.

formulas.name: Capacitance of an isolated sphere
formulas.note: R radius of the sphere.

formulas.name: RC discharge
formulas.note: Charging: Q = Q₀(1 − e^(−t/RC)). τ in seconds when R in Ω and C in F.

shortcuts.name: Coulomb scaling
shortcuts.rule: F ∝ q₁q₂/r²: multiply by the change in each charge and divide by the square of the change in distance.
shortcuts.example: F = 36 N. Both charges doubled and distance tripled: 36 × (2 × 2)/3² = 36 × 4/9 = 16 N.

shortcuts.name: Identical and paired capacitors
shortcuts.rule: n identical capacitors C: series C/n, parallel nC. Two in series: product over sum.
shortcuts.example: Four 8 μF in series = 2 μF; in parallel = 32 μF. 3 μF and 6 μF in series = 18/9 = 2 μF.

shortcuts.name: Series voltage split
shortcuts.rule: In series the smaller capacitor takes the larger voltage: V divides in inverse ratio of C.
shortcuts.example: 3 μF and 6 μF in series across 12 V: ratio of voltages 2 : 1, so 8 V across 3 μF and 4 V across 6 μF. Check: Q = 2 μF × 12 V = 24 μC; 24/3 = 8, 24/6 = 4.

shortcuts.name: Connected or isolated?
shortcuts.rule: Still connected to the battery: V is constant. Disconnected: Q is constant. Then use C ∝ εᵣA/d.
shortcuts.example: Isolated capacitor, plate separation doubled: C halves, V = Q/C doubles, energy Q²/(2C) doubles. Same change with battery connected: C halves, Q halves, energy ½CV² halves.

shortcuts.name: Charge sharing on touching
shortcuts.rule: Two identical conducting spheres that touch end with half the total charge each.
shortcuts.example: +8 μC and −2 μC touch: each gets (8 − 2)/2 = +3 μC. Force changes from attractive with product 16 to repulsive with product 9, so its size becomes 9/16 of the original.

shortcuts.name: Time-constant percentages
shortcuts.rule: After one τ = RC: a charging capacitor reaches 63% of full charge; a discharging one keeps 37%. After 5τ it is effectively complete.
shortcuts.example: R = 10 kΩ, C = 100 μF: τ = 10⁴ × 10⁻⁴ = 1 s. After 1 s discharge about 37% of the charge is left; after about 5 s it is nearly empty.

traps: Adding capacitors in series like resistors (C₁ + C₂); for capacitors that is the parallel rule.
Adding potentials as vectors; potential is a scalar, field is the vector.
Forgetting μF and pF prefixes: 2 μF = 2 × 10⁻⁶ F.
Assuming the field inside a hollow charged conductor is non-zero.
Using ½CV² when the capacitor is isolated and V is changing; Q²/(2C) is easier because Q is fixed.
nsmqTips: Spot first whether the question keeps Q or V constant; that decides every ratio.
Capacitor networks in NSMQ are usually symmetric or use nice numbers (2, 3, 6 μF); collapse them step by step in your head.
Riddle clues: 'the region around a charge where it feels a force' (electric field), 'two conductors separated by an insulator' (capacitor), 'gold-leaf electroscope'.
State units for answers: farad, coulomb, volt, N/C or V/m.

topics.strand: Electric Field, Magnetic Field and Electronics
topics.summary: Current electricity deals with the flow of charge, resistance, e.m.f., power and circuit analysis using Ohm's and Kirchhoff's laws. It is one of the most reliable sources of NSMQ calculation questions, especially resistor networks, internal resistance and the cost of electrical energy.
keyIdeas: Current is the rate of flow of charge; conventional current flows from + to −, opposite to electron flow.
Ohm's law (V ∝ I at constant temperature) holds for metallic conductors; filament lamps and diodes are non-ohmic.
In series the current is the same everywhere and resistances add; in parallel the p.d. is the same and conductances (1/R) add.
E.m.f. is the energy given per coulomb by the source; terminal p.d. is less than e.m.f. when current flows because of internal resistance.
Kirchhoff's first law (junction rule) expresses conservation of charge; the second (loop rule) expresses conservation of energy.
Metal resistance rises with temperature; semiconductor (thermistor) resistance falls.
An ideal ammeter has zero resistance and goes in series; an ideal voltmeter has infinite resistance and goes in parallel.
The kilowatt-hour (kWh) is a unit of energy: 1 kWh = 3.6 × 10⁶ J.

formulas.name: Ohm's law
formulas.note: R in ohms (Ω).

formulas.name: Resistivity
formulas.note: ρ resistivity (Ω m), L length, A cross-sectional area.

formulas.name: Series and parallel resistors
formulas.note: Two in parallel: R = R₁R₂/(R₁ + R₂).

formulas.name: Electrical power
formulas.note: Use I²R when current is common (series), V²/R when voltage is common (parallel).

formulas.name: Electrical energy
formulas.note: Joules if t in s; kWh if P in kW and t in h.

formulas.name: E.m.f. and internal resistance
formulas.formula: E = I(R + r), V = E − Ir
formulas.note: r internal resistance, V terminal p.d.

formulas.name: Maximum power transfer
formulas.formula: P is maximum when R = r; P_max = E²/(4r)
formulas.note: Efficiency at that point is only 50%.

formulas.name: Wheatstone bridge balance
formulas.note: Galvanometer reads zero; metre bridge: R/S = l/(100 − l).

formulas.name: Potentiometer comparison of e.m.f.s
formulas.note: l balance lengths; no current drawn from the cell at balance.

formulas.name: Temperature dependence of resistance
formulas.note: α temperature coefficient of resistance, θ in °C.

formulas.name: Drift velocity
formulas.note: n charge carriers per m³, v drift speed, q = e for electrons.

shortcuts.name: Parallel pairs and identical sets
shortcuts.rule: Two in parallel: product over sum. n identical R in parallel: R/n. Parallel total is always less than the smallest resistor.
shortcuts.example: 6 Ω ∥ 3 Ω = 18/9 = 2 Ω. Five 10 Ω in parallel = 2 Ω. 4 Ω ∥ 12 Ω = 48/16 = 3 Ω.

shortcuts.name: Stretching and cutting wires
shortcuts.rule: Stretch to n times the length (volume fixed): R becomes n²R. Cut into n equal pieces and connect them in parallel: R becomes R/n².
shortcuts.example: A 4 Ω wire stretched to double length: 4 × 4 = 16 Ω. A 12 Ω wire cut in half and the halves joined in parallel: 12/4 = 3 Ω.

shortcuts.name: Which bulb glows brighter?
shortcuts.rule: For bulbs with the same voltage rating, R = V²/P, so the lower-wattage bulb has the bigger resistance and glows brighter in series (P = I²R); in parallel the higher-wattage bulb is brighter.
shortcuts.example: 240 V, 60 W bulb: R = 57600/60 = 960 Ω. 240 V, 100 W bulb: R = 576 Ω. In series the 60 W bulb is brighter.

shortcuts.name: Cost of electricity
shortcuts.rule: Units (kWh) = kW × hours; cost = units × tariff.
shortcuts.example: A 2 kW heater used 3 h a day for 30 days: 2 × 3 × 30 = 180 kWh. At 1.50 cedis per kWh the cost is 270 cedis.

shortcuts.name: Internal resistance from 'lost volts'
shortcuts.rule: r = (E − V)/I: the drop in terminal p.d. divided by the current.
shortcuts.example: Cell e.m.f. 12 V, terminal p.d. 10 V while delivering 2 A: r = 2/2 = 1 Ω. Maximum power it can deliver to a load: E²/(4r) = 144/4 = 36 W.

shortcuts.name: Balanced bridge symmetry
shortcuts.rule: If the ratios across a bridge match, the middle resistor carries no current and can be removed.
shortcuts.example: Arms 2 Ω and 4 Ω on top, 3 Ω and 6 Ω below, a 5 Ω resistor across the middle: 2/4 = 3/6, so remove the 5 Ω. Total = (2 + 4) ∥ (3 + 6) = 6 ∥ 9 = 54/15 = 3.6 Ω.

traps: Calling the kilowatt-hour a unit of power; it is energy.
Using P = V²/R for series components where the current, not the voltage, is shared.
Forgetting internal resistance when the question gives one; terminal p.d. is not equal to e.m.f.
Putting a voltmeter in series or an ammeter in parallel.
Assuming every component obeys Ohm's law; filament lamps and diodes do not.
nsmqTips: Redraw messy networks mentally: find points at the same potential and collapse parallel groups first.
Have R = V²/P ready for bulb and heater questions; ratings are usually 240 V or 12 V.
In riddles, 'opposition to flow of current', 'energy per unit charge' and 'rate of flow of charge' are standard definitions; answer with the exact term.
Check the answer's size: a parallel combination cannot exceed its smallest branch.

topics.strand: Electric Field, Magnetic Field and Electronics
topics.summary: This topic covers magnets, magnetic fields, the fields produced by currents and the forces on currents and moving charges in magnetic fields. NSMQ asks about direction rules, field formulas for wires and solenoids, charged-particle paths and converting galvanometers into meters.
keyIdeas: Like poles repel, unlike poles attract; field lines run from N to S outside a magnet and never cross.
The Earth's geographic North Pole is near a magnetic south pole, which is why a compass N-pole points north.
A current-carrying conductor produces a magnetic field; its direction follows the right-hand grip rule.
A conductor carrying current across a magnetic field feels a force given by Fleming's left-hand rule; this is the motor effect.
The magnetic force on a moving charge is always perpendicular to its velocity, so it changes direction but does no work and the speed stays constant.
Soft iron (easily magnetised and demagnetised) is used for electromagnets and transformer cores; steel (retains magnetism) for permanent magnets.
Ferromagnetic materials lose their magnetism above the Curie temperature.
Parallel currents in the same direction attract; opposite directions repel.

formulas.name: Force on a current-carrying conductor
formulas.note: B flux density (T), L length in the field, θ angle between wire and field.

formulas.name: Force on a moving charge
formulas.note: θ angle between velocity and field. Zero when moving parallel to B.

formulas.name: Radius of circular path
formulas.note: Charge moving perpendicular to a uniform field.

formulas.name: Period of circular motion in a field
formulas.note: Independent of speed (basis of the cyclotron).

formulas.name: Field of a long straight wire
formulas.note: μ₀ = 4π × 10⁻⁷ T m A⁻¹, r distance from the wire.

formulas.name: Field at centre of a circular coil
formulas.note: N turns, R radius.

formulas.name: Field inside a long solenoid
formulas.note: n turns per metre (N/L). Multiply by μᵣ for an iron core.

formulas.name: Force between parallel wires
formulas.note: d separation; basis of the former definition of the ampere.

formulas.name: Torque on a rectangular coil
formulas.note: θ angle between B and the normal to the coil; maximum when the coil plane is parallel to B.

formulas.name: Velocity selector
formulas.note: Crossed electric and magnetic fields; only particles of this speed pass undeflected.

formulas.name: Shunt for an ammeter
formulas.note: Small resistor in parallel with the galvanometer; I full-scale current required.

formulas.name: Multiplier for a voltmeter
formulas.note: Large resistor in series with the galvanometer; V full-scale voltage required.

shortcuts.name: μ₀/(2π) = 2 × 10⁻⁷
shortcuts.rule: Wire field B = 2 × 10⁻⁷ × I/r and force per metre between wires = 2 × 10⁻⁷ × I₁I₂/d.

shortcuts.name: Range-extension factor n
shortcuts.rule: To make the range n times bigger: ammeter shunt R_s = r_g/(n − 1); voltmeter multiplier R_m = (n − 1)r_g.
shortcuts.example: Galvanometer 50 Ω, full scale 1 mA. As a 10 mA ammeter (n = 10): R_s = 50/9 ≈ 5.6 Ω. As a 1 V voltmeter (galvanometer full scale is 0.05 V, so n = 20): R_m = 19 × 50 = 950 Ω.

shortcuts.name: Radius comparison of particles
shortcuts.rule: r = mv/(qB). Same speed: r ∝ m/q. Same kinetic energy: r ∝ √m/q.
shortcuts.example: Proton (m = 1, q = 1) and alpha (m = 4, q = 2) at the same speed: alpha radius is 4/2 = 2 times bigger. At the same kinetic energy: √4/2 = 1, so the radii are equal.

shortcuts.name: Fleming's left-hand rule mnemonic
shortcuts.rule: thuMb = Motion (force), First finger = Field, seCond finger = Current. For electrons point the second finger opposite to their motion.
shortcuts.example: Field into the page, current to the right: force on the wire is up the page. An electron moving right in the same field is pushed down the page.

shortcuts.name: Zero-force check
shortcuts.rule: If the current or velocity is parallel to B, the force is zero; if a charge moves in a magnetic field only, its kinetic energy never changes.
shortcuts.example: An electron fired along a solenoid's axis goes straight through undeflected. A proton circling in a 0.5 T field keeps exactly the same speed.

traps: Using the right-hand rule for force on a conductor (that is for induced current); the motor effect uses the left hand.
Forgetting to reverse the direction for negative charges such as electrons.
Saying a magnetic field speeds up a charged particle; it only changes its direction.
Using total turns N instead of turns per metre n in B = μ₀nI.
Thinking the compass N-pole points to a magnetic north pole; it points to a magnetic south pole in the Arctic.
nsmqTips: Many questions only need the direction: picture the hand rule and answer 'into the page', 'upwards', and so on.
Remember 4π × 10⁻⁷ and 2 × 10⁻⁷; they shorten almost every field calculation.
Riddles mention 'domains', 'Curie point', 'hysteresis', 'soft iron', 'solenoid' or 'electric bell'; link each to magnetism quickly.
For shunt and multiplier questions, state 'small resistor in parallel' or 'large resistor in series' even before calculating.

topics.strand: Electric Field, Magnetic Field and Electronics
topics.summary: Electromagnetic induction is the production of e.m.f. by a changing magnetic flux, the principle behind generators, transformers and power transmission. NSMQ asks about Faraday's and Lenz's laws, transformer ratios, r.m.s. values, reactance and resonance.
keyIdeas: Faraday's law: induced e.m.f. equals the rate of change of flux linkage.
Lenz's law: the induced current flows so as to oppose the change that causes it (a consequence of energy conservation).
Fleming's right-hand rule gives the direction of induced current in a moving conductor (generator rule).
In an a.c. generator the e.m.f. is maximum when the coil plane is parallel to the field (flux zero, changing fastest) and zero when the flux is maximum.
Transformers work only with a.c.; laminated soft-iron cores reduce eddy-current losses.
Power is transmitted at high voltage and low current to reduce I²R losses in the cables.
In a pure capacitor current leads voltage by 90°; in a pure inductor voltage leads current by 90°; in a resistor they are in phase.
At resonance in a series LCR circuit X_L = X_C, impedance is minimum (Z = R) and current is maximum.

formulas.name: Magnetic flux
formulas.note: Unit weber (Wb); θ angle between B and the normal to the area. Flux linkage = NΦ.

formulas.name: Faraday–Lenz law
formulas.note: Minus sign expresses Lenz's law.

formulas.name: E.m.f. in a moving rod
formulas.note: Rod of length L moving at speed v perpendicular to B.

formulas.name: A.c. generator
formulas.formula: e = E₀ sin ωt, E₀ = NBAω
formulas.note: ω = 2πf angular speed of the coil.

formulas.name: Ideal transformer
formulas.note: Step-up when Nₛ > Nₚ. Assumes 100% efficiency.

formulas.name: Transformer efficiency
formulas.note: Losses: copper (I²R), eddy currents, hysteresis, flux leakage.

formulas.name: Root-mean-square values
formulas.note: Sinusoidal a.c. only. Mean power P = V_rms I_rms for a resistor.

formulas.name: Inductive reactance
formulas.note: L inductance in henry (H).

formulas.name: Capacitive reactance
formulas.note: C in farad.

formulas.name: Impedance of series LCR
formulas.note: I_rms = V_rms/Z; tan φ = (X_L − X_C)/R.

formulas.name: Resonant frequency
formulas.note: Used for tuning radio receivers.

formulas.name: Self-induction and stored energy
formulas.note: Energy stored in the magnetic field of an inductor.

shortcuts.name: Peak and r.m.s. in one multiplication
shortcuts.example: Mains 230 V r.m.s.: peak ≈ 230 × 1.414 ≈ 325 V. 240 V mains: peak ≈ 339 V. Peak current 10 A: r.m.s. ≈ 7.07 A.

shortcuts.name: Turns ratio does everything
shortcuts.rule: Voltage scales by Nₛ/Nₚ; current scales by the inverse ratio.
shortcuts.example: Nₚ = 1000, Nₛ = 50, input 240 V: ratio 1/20, so output 12 V. If the secondary draws 2 A, the primary draws 2/20 = 0.1 A (ideal).

shortcuts.name: Transmission loss scales as 1/V²
shortcuts.rule: For the same power, raising the voltage n times cuts the current n times and the I²R loss n² times.
shortcuts.example: Stepping up from 10 kV to 100 kV (n = 10) cuts cable loss by a factor of 100: a 50 kW loss becomes 0.5 kW.

shortcuts.name: Reactance with frequency
shortcuts.rule: X_L ∝ f, X_C ∝ 1/f. On steady d.c. (f = 0) an inductor acts as a plain wire and a capacitor as a break.
shortcuts.example: A coil with X_L = 30 Ω at 50 Hz has 60 Ω at 100 Hz. A capacitor with X_C = 30 Ω at 50 Hz has 15 Ω at 100 Hz.

shortcuts.name: Phase mnemonic CIVIL
shortcuts.rule: CIVIL: in C, I leads V; V leads I in L. Equivalent: ELI the ICE man.
shortcuts.example: In a circuit containing only a capacitor, current peaks a quarter cycle (90°) before voltage.

shortcuts.name: Resonance with nice numbers
shortcuts.rule: Pick L and C so that LC is a perfect square power of ten, then f₀ = 1/(2π√LC) ≈ 0.159/√LC.

traps: Saying a transformer can step up d.c.; a constant current produces no changing flux.
Confusing r.m.s. with average: average over a full cycle is zero, over a half cycle is 0.637 × peak.
Thinking generator e.m.f. is largest when flux through the coil is largest; it is largest when flux is changing fastest (flux zero).
Applying the left-hand rule to generators; induced current uses the right-hand rule.
Assuming a step-up transformer gives more power out; voltage rises but current falls, and power out ≤ power in.
nsmqTips: Transformer questions are almost always a one-step ratio; say the ratio aloud and scale.
Have 1.414 and 0.707 ready; mains questions (230 V or 240 V, 50 Hz in Ghana) are common.
For Lenz's law questions, answer as 'the coil face becomes a N-pole to repel the approaching N-pole', which is quicker than drawing.
Riddle clues: 'laminated core', 'slip rings', 'commutator', 'eddy currents', 'back e.m.f.'.

topics.strand: Electric Field, Magnetic Field and Electronics
topics.summary: This topic covers semiconductor materials, doping, p-n junction diodes, rectification, transistors, operational amplifiers and logic gates. NSMQ uses it for definition questions, truth tables and quick calculations of transistor gain and diode currents.
keyIdeas: Pure (intrinsic) silicon and germanium are group 14 elements whose conductivity rises with temperature as more electron–hole pairs form.

n-type material is doped with a group 15 donor (P, As, Sb) and has electrons as majority carriers; p-type is doped with a group 13 acceptor (B, Al, Ga, In) and has holes as majority carriers. Both remain electrically neutral.
A p-n junction forms a depletion layer; forward bias (p to +) narrows it and current flows, reverse bias widens it and almost no current flows.
A diode acts as a rectifier; a bridge of four diodes gives full-wave rectification, and a capacitor smooths the output.
A Zener diode is designed to conduct in reverse at a fixed breakdown voltage and is used as a voltage regulator.
A bipolar transistor (npn or pnp) uses a small base current to control a larger collector current; it can be an amplifier or a switch.
NAND and NOR are universal gates: any logic circuit can be built from only one of them.
LEDs emit light when forward biased; photodiodes and LDRs respond to light.

formulas.name: Barrier (turn-on) voltage
formulas.note: Forward voltage drop across a conducting diode.

formulas.name: Diode circuit current
formulas.note: V_D ≈ 0.7 V for silicon; R series resistor.

formulas.name: Transistor currents
formulas.note: Kirchhoff's junction rule applied to the transistor.

formulas.name: Common-emitter current gain
formulas.note: Typically 50–300; also written h_FE.

formulas.name: Common-base current gain
formulas.note: α is slightly less than 1.

formulas.name: Voltage gain
formulas.formula: A_v = V_out/V_in, gain in dB = 20 log₁₀ A_v
formulas.note: Power gain in dB = 10 log₁₀(P_out/P_in).

formulas.name: Inverting op-amp amplifier
formulas.note: Output is 180° out of phase with input.

formulas.name: Non-inverting op-amp amplifier
formulas.note: Output in phase with input.

formulas.name: Rectifier average output
formulas.note: V₀ peak voltage (ideal diodes).

formulas.name: Ripple frequency
formulas.note: f supply frequency.

formulas.name: Zener series resistor
formulas.note: I total current through R (Zener plus load).

formulas.name: Boolean expressions of gates
formulas.formula: AND: A·B; OR: A + B; NOT: Ā; NAND: (A·B)‾; NOR: (A + B)‾; XOR: A ⊕ B
formulas.note: XOR gives 1 when the inputs differ.

shortcuts.name: β straight from α
shortcuts.rule: β = α/(1 − α): divide α by what is left over from 1.

shortcuts.name: Gate outputs by one rule each
shortcuts.rule: AND is 1 only if all inputs are 1; OR is 0 only if all inputs are 0; NAND and NOR are the inverses; XOR is 1 when an odd number of inputs are 1.
shortcuts.example: Inputs A = 1, B = 0: AND 0, OR 1, NAND 1, NOR 0, XOR 1, XNOR 0.

shortcuts.name: Tie the inputs
shortcuts.rule: A NAND or NOR gate with its inputs joined works as a NOT gate (De Morgan: (A·B)‾ = Ā + B̄ and (A + B)‾ = Ā·B̄).
shortcuts.example: To make a NOT gate from NAND only, join both inputs: input 1 gives output 0, input 0 gives output 1.

shortcuts.name: Dopant mnemonic
shortcuts.rule: n-type 'PAS' (Phosphorus, Arsenic, antimony Sb: group 15, five valence electrons, one spare electron). p-type 'BAGI' (Boron, Aluminium, Gallium, Indium: group 13, three valence electrons, one hole).
shortcuts.example: Silicon doped with gallium: Ga is in BAGI, so the material is p-type with holes as majority carriers.

shortcuts.name: Subtract 0.7 V first
shortcuts.rule: For a forward-biased silicon diode, remove 0.7 V from the supply, then use Ohm's law on the resistor.
shortcuts.example: 5 V supply, 1 kΩ resistor, silicon diode forward biased: I = (5 − 0.7)/1000 = 4.3 mA. Reverse it: I ≈ 0.

shortcuts.name: Op-amp gain in one glance
shortcuts.rule: Inverting gain = −R_f/R_in; non-inverting = that ratio plus 1.
shortcuts.example: R_f = 100 kΩ, R_in = 10 kΩ: inverting gain −10, non-inverting +11. A 0.2 V input gives −2 V or +2.2 V.

traps: Calling n-type material negatively charged; doped semiconductors are neutral overall.
Thinking semiconductor resistance rises with temperature like a metal; it falls.
Confusing ripple frequencies: a full-wave rectifier on 50 Hz mains gives 100 Hz ripple, not 50 Hz.
Writing I_C = I_B + I_E; the emitter current is the largest: I_E = I_B + I_C.
Mixing up NAND and NOR outputs for inputs 1, 0: NAND gives 1, NOR gives 0.
nsmqTips: Truth-table questions are quickest with the one-line rules above; do not build the full table unless asked.
Expect definitions such as 'majority carriers', 'depletion layer', 'forward bias', 'doping'; answer with the exact term.
Riddle clues: 'universal gate' (NAND or NOR), 'light-emitting', 'voltage regulator' (Zener), 'three terminals: emitter, base, collector' (transistor).
For transistor switches, remember that a small base current turns on a large collector current; the base current is usually tens of microamps.

topics.summary: This topic covers the structure of the atom, energy levels and spectra, the photoelectric effect, X-rays and wave–particle duality. NSMQ questions test photon energies, hydrogen energy levels, the photoelectric equation and de Broglie wavelength, often with quick electronvolt arithmetic.
keyIdeas: Rutherford's alpha-scattering experiment showed a tiny, dense, positive nucleus; most of the atom is empty space.
In Bohr's model electrons occupy discrete energy levels; they emit or absorb a photon whose energy equals the difference between levels.
Emission spectra are bright lines on a dark background; absorption spectra are dark lines on a continuous spectrum, at the same wavelengths.
Hydrogen series: Lyman (ending on n = 1, ultraviolet), Balmer (n = 2, visible), Paschen (n = 3, infrared).
Photoelectric effect: emission happens only above a threshold frequency; maximum kinetic energy depends on frequency, while the number of electrons depends on intensity; emission is instantaneous.
Light behaves as particles (photons) in the photoelectric effect and as waves in interference; electrons show wave behaviour in diffraction.
X-rays are produced when fast electrons strike a metal target; the shortest wavelength is set by the accelerating voltage.

formulas.name: Einstein's photoelectric equation
formulas.note: φ work function. KE_max = ½mv²_max.

formulas.name: Stopping potential
formulas.note: V_s is numerically equal to KE_max in eV.

formulas.name: Threshold frequency and wavelength
formulas.note: No emission if f < f₀ (λ > λ₀), whatever the intensity.

formulas.name: de Broglie wavelength
formulas.note: K kinetic energy. For an electron through V volts, K = eV.

formulas.name: Hydrogen energy levels
formulas.note: Ground state n = 1; ionisation energy 13.6 eV.

formulas.name: Photon from a transition
formulas.note: Emission when falling, absorption when rising.

formulas.name: Bohr radius and angular momentum
formulas.formula: rₙ = n²a₀, a₀ ≈ 0.053 nm; L = nh/(2π)
formulas.note: Hydrogen atom.

formulas.name: Minimum X-ray wavelength
formulas.note: V accelerating voltage of the tube (Duane–Hunt law).

formulas.name: Useful constant
formulas.note: Lets you convert between eV and nm instantly.

formulas.name: Number of possible emission lines
formulas.note: Electron starting in level n and falling by all possible routes.

shortcuts.name: 1240 rule
shortcuts.rule: Photon energy in eV = 1240 ÷ wavelength in nm (and the reverse).

shortcuts.name: Hydrogen level ladder
shortcuts.rule: Learn −13.6, −3.4, −1.51, −0.85 eV for n = 1 to 4; differences give the lines.

shortcuts.name: Counting spectral lines
shortcuts.rule: From level n the number of different lines is n(n − 1)/2.
shortcuts.example: From n = 4: 4 × 3/2 = 6 lines. From n = 5: 10 lines.

shortcuts.name: Photoelectric in electronvolts
shortcuts.rule: Work everything in eV: KE_max = (1240/λ) − φ, and the stopping potential in volts is the same number.
shortcuts.example: λ = 310 nm, φ = 2.3 eV: photon energy 1240/310 = 4.0 eV, KE_max = 1.7 eV, stopping potential 1.7 V.

shortcuts.name: Electron de Broglie wavelength
shortcuts.rule: For an electron accelerated through V volts, λ ≈ 1.23/√V nm.
shortcuts.example: V = 100 V: λ ≈ 1.23/10 = 0.123 nm, similar to atomic spacing, so electrons diffract from crystals.

shortcuts.name: X-ray cut-off
shortcuts.rule: λ_min in nm = 1240 ÷ (voltage in volts).

traps: Saying brighter light gives faster photoelectrons; intensity changes the number of electrons, frequency changes their energy.
Forgetting to convert eV to joules (× 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹) when using SI formulas.
Mixing up threshold frequency (minimum) with threshold wavelength (maximum).
Leaving out the minus sign in hydrogen energies, or giving ionisation energy as negative.
Writing the Rydberg formula with n₁ and n₂ the wrong way round, which gives a negative wavelength.
nsmqTips: Almost every numerical here is fastest in eV and nm with hc = 1240 eV nm.
Memorise the visible range (about 400 to 700 nm, 1.8 to 3.1 eV); questions often ask which series or region a line belongs to.
Riddle clues: 'gold foil' (Rutherford), 'quantised orbits' (Bohr), 'matter waves' (de Broglie), 'work function' (photoelectric).
When asked what changes with intensity versus frequency, answer in one line: intensity → current; frequency → KE_max.

topics.summary: This topic covers nuclear structure, radioactive decay, half-life, nuclear equations, binding energy, fission and fusion. NSMQ often sets half-life fractions, decay-chain counting and the properties of alpha, beta and gamma radiation.
keyIdeas: A nucleus is described by mass number A (protons + neutrons) and atomic number Z (protons); isotopes have the same Z but different A.
Alpha particles are helium nuclei (⁴₂He): strongly ionising, weakly penetrating, stopped by paper or a few cm of air.
Beta-minus particles are fast electrons from a neutron changing into a proton; they are stopped by a few mm of aluminium.
Gamma rays are high-energy photons: weakly ionising, very penetrating, reduced by thick lead or concrete, and not deflected by fields.
Radioactive decay is random and spontaneous, not affected by temperature, pressure or chemical state.
Binding energy per nucleon peaks near iron-56 (about 8.8 MeV); heavy nuclei release energy by fission, light nuclei by fusion.
In a nuclear reaction both mass number and atomic number (charge) are conserved.

formulas.name: Decay law
formulas.note: λ decay constant (s⁻¹), N undecayed nuclei.

formulas.name: Half-life form
formulas.note: Easiest form when t is a whole number of half-lives.

formulas.name: Half-life and decay constant
formulas.note: Mean life τ = 1/λ = 1.44 T½.

formulas.name: Activity
formulas.note: Unit becquerel (Bq) = 1 decay per second.

formulas.name: Alpha decay
formulas.note: A falls by 4, Z falls by 2.

formulas.name: Beta-minus and beta-plus decay
formulas.note: A unchanged in both.

formulas.name: Gamma emission
formulas.note: A and Z unchanged; the nucleus loses excess energy.

formulas.name: Mass defect and binding energy
formulas.formula: Δm = Zmₚ + (A − Z)mₙ − M_nucleus; BE = Δm c²
formulas.note: Binding energy per nucleon = BE/A.

formulas.name: Nuclear radius
formulas.note: Nuclear density is about the same for all nuclei.

formulas.name: Counting α and β in a chain
formulas.formula: Number of α = ΔA/4; number of β⁻ = 2(number of α) − ΔZ
formulas.note: ΔA and ΔZ are the total drops from parent to final daughter.

formulas.name: Gamma absorption
formulas.formula: I = I₀ e^(−μx), half-value thickness x½ = 0.693/μ
formulas.note: μ linear attenuation coefficient.

shortcuts.name: Halving chain
shortcuts.rule: After n half-lives the fraction left is 1/2ⁿ: 1/2, 1/4, 1/8, 1/16, 1/32 …
shortcuts.example: 64 g of a nuclide with T½ = 2 days, after 6 days (3 half-lives): 64 → 32 → 16 → 8 g left; 56 g (7/8) has decayed.

shortcuts.name: Age from fraction remaining
shortcuts.rule: Turn the fraction into a power of 2, then multiply by the half-life.
shortcuts.example: 1/16 of a sample remains and T½ = 5 days: 16 = 2⁴, so 4 half-lives = 20 days old.

shortcuts.name: Decay-chain counting
shortcuts.rule: α from the mass drop, then β from the leftover charge.
shortcuts.example: ²³⁸₉₂U → ²⁰⁶₈₂Pb: ΔA = 32, so 8 α. 8 α lower Z by 16 (to 76), but Z only fell by 10, so 16 − 10 = 6 β⁻ decays.

shortcuts.name: 931 MeV per u
shortcuts.rule: Multiply the mass defect in u by 931.5 for MeV; divide by A for per-nucleon value.
shortcuts.example: He-4 mass defect 0.0304 u: BE ≈ 0.0304 × 931.5 ≈ 28.3 MeV, per nucleon ≈ 7.1 MeV.

shortcuts.name: Cube-root radius
shortcuts.rule: R ∝ A^(1/3): pick perfect cubes.
shortcuts.example: Al-27: R = 1.2 × 3 = 3.6 fm. A nucleus with A = 216 has radius 2 times that of A = 27 (since 216/27 = 8 = 2³).

shortcuts.name: λ from T½ with 693
shortcuts.rule: λ = 0.693/T½: choose numbers that cancel 693.
shortcuts.example: T½ = 693 s → λ = 1.0 × 10⁻³ s⁻¹. With N = 10²⁰ nuclei, activity = 10¹⁷ Bq.

traps: Thinking the sample is gone after two half-lives; a quarter remains.
Saying beta particles are orbital electrons; they come from the nucleus.
Changing A or Z for gamma emission.
Assuming heating or compressing a sample changes its half-life.
Putting fusion on the heavy side of the binding-energy curve; fusion releases energy for light nuclei, fission for heavy ones.
nsmqTips: Half-life questions are almost always designed to give whole numbers of half-lives; count the halvings out loud.
For nuclear equations, balance A on top and Z at the bottom; the missing particle is whatever closes both sums.
Know the penetration and ionisation order (α > β > γ for ionising, the reverse for penetrating) and the deflection rules in fields.
Riddle clues: 'Becquerel', 'Curies', 'chain reaction', 'moderator', 'control rods', 'carbon dating (T½ ≈ 5730 years)'.

topics.summary: Special relativity describes physics at speeds close to that of light, predicting time dilation, length contraction and mass–energy equivalence, and modern physics extends this to photon momentum and Compton scattering. In NSMQ it appears in harder rounds, where knowing standard γ values and limiting cases lets you answer in seconds.
keyIdeas: Einstein's postulates: the laws of physics are the same in all inertial frames, and the speed of light in vacuum is the same for all inertial observers.
Moving clocks run slow (time dilation); proper time is measured by a clock at rest relative to the events.
Moving objects are shorter along the direction of motion only (length contraction); proper length is measured in the object's rest frame.
Events simultaneous in one frame need not be simultaneous in another.
No object with mass can reach c, because its energy would become infinite.
Rest energy E₀ = mc²: electron 0.511 MeV, proton 938 MeV.
Photons have zero rest mass but carry momentum p = E/c; Compton scattering of X-rays by electrons confirms this.
At low speeds all relativistic formulas reduce to Newtonian ones.

formulas.name: Lorentz factor
formulas.note: γ ≥ 1; γ = 1 at rest.

formulas.name: Time dilation
formulas.note: Δt₀ proper time.

formulas.name: Length contraction
formulas.note: L₀ proper length, contraction along motion only.

formulas.name: Relativistic momentum
formulas.note: m rest mass.

formulas.name: Total and kinetic energy
formulas.note: Not ½γmv².

formulas.name: Energy–momentum relation
formulas.note: For a photon m = 0, so E = pc.

formulas.name: Velocity addition
formulas.note: Speeds along the same line; result never exceeds c.

formulas.name: Relativistic Doppler (approaching)
formulas.note: Use (1 − β)/(1 + β) for receding (redshift).

formulas.name: Photon momentum
formulas.note: Radiation pressure on a surface comes from this.

formulas.name: Compton shift
formulas.note: θ scattering angle of the photon.

formulas.name: Pair production threshold
formulas.note: Needs a nearby nucleus to conserve momentum.

formulas.name: Schwarzschild radius
formulas.note: Event horizon radius of a non-rotating black hole.

shortcuts.name: Standard γ values
shortcuts.rule: 0.6c → γ = 1.25; 0.8c → γ = 5/3; 0.866c (√3/2 c) → γ = 2; 0.98c → γ ≈ 5. The first two come from the 3-4-5 triangle.
shortcuts.example: A muon with proper lifetime 2.2 μs at 0.8c lives 2.2 × 5/3 ≈ 3.67 μs in the lab. A 100 m rocket at 0.6c measures 100/1.25 = 80 m.

shortcuts.name: 3-4-5 energy triangle
shortcuts.rule: E² = (pc)² + (mc²)² is a right triangle with hypotenuse E. For γ = 5/3: E = 5/3 mc², pc = 4/3 mc², KE = 2/3 mc².

shortcuts.name: KE equals rest energy means γ = 2
shortcuts.rule: If KE = mc², then γ − 1 = 1, so γ = 2 and v = 0.866c.
shortcuts.example: An electron accelerated through 511 kV gains 0.511 MeV = its rest energy, so it moves at about 0.866c.

shortcuts.name: Velocity addition limits
shortcuts.rule: Anything combined with c gives c; two speeds of 0.5c give 0.8c, not c.
shortcuts.example: 0.5c + 0.5c: (1.0c)/(1 + 0.25) = 0.8c. Light emitted forward from a ship at 0.9c still travels at c.

shortcuts.name: Low-speed check
shortcuts.rule: γ ≈ 1 + v²/(2c²) for v ≪ c, so KE ≈ ½mv². Use it to test whether relativity matters.
shortcuts.example: v = 0.1c: γ ≈ 1 + 0.01/2 = 1.005 (exact 1.00504), only 0.5% different, so Newtonian answers are fine.

shortcuts.name: Compton at key angles
shortcuts.rule: Shift = 2.43 pm × (1 − cos θ): 0 at 0°, 2.43 pm at 90°, 4.86 pm (maximum) at 180°.
shortcuts.example: A 0.100 nm X-ray scattered at 90° comes out at 0.100 + 0.00243 ≈ 0.1024 nm.

traps: Assigning proper time to the wrong observer; it is the clock at rest with respect to the events.
Contracting lengths perpendicular to the motion.
Writing KE = ½γmv² or ½mv² at high speed; use (γ − 1)mc².
Adding velocities by simple addition and getting more than c.
Treating 'relativistic mass' as rest mass in E² = (pc)² + (mc²)²; m there is the rest mass.
nsmqTips: Questions are built around 0.6c, 0.8c and 0.866c; recognise them and use the γ values directly.
Do a limiting-case check aloud: if v → 0 the result should become Newtonian; if v → c, γ → ∞.
Quote rest energies (electron 0.511 MeV, proton 938 MeV) from memory; they turn most energy questions into one multiplication.
Riddle clues: 'twin paradox', 'muon reaching sea level', 'Michelson–Morley', 'event horizon'.

topics.summary: This topic links gravitation and radiation to the Earth, its atmosphere, the solar system and the wider universe, including satellites, seasons, the structure of the Earth and how stars radiate. NSMQ uses it for recall questions on layers and planets and for ratio questions on orbits, gravity and radiation.
keyIdeas: Seasons are caused by the tilt of the Earth's axis (about 23.5°), not by changes in its distance from the Sun.

The atmosphere's layers from the ground up are troposphere (weather, temperature falls with height), stratosphere (ozone layer absorbs UV), mesosphere, thermosphere (ionosphere, aurora) and exosphere.
The greenhouse effect: the Earth absorbs short-wavelength solar radiation and emits long-wavelength infrared, part of which is absorbed by CO₂, water vapour and methane.
Seismic P-waves are longitudinal and pass through solids and liquids; S-waves are transverse and cannot pass through liquids, which shows the outer core is liquid.
A geostationary satellite orbits above the equator, west to east, with a period of 24 h at about 36 000 km altitude.
Astronauts in orbit feel weightless because they are in free fall, not because gravity is absent.
The Sun produces energy by nuclear fusion of hydrogen into helium; distant galaxies show a redshift, evidence that the universe is expanding.

formulas.name: Newton's law of gravitation
formulas.note: G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻²; r between centres.

formulas.name: Surface gravity
formulas.note: Earth: g ≈ 9.8 m/s², R ≈ 6.4 × 10⁶ m, M ≈ 6.0 × 10²⁴ kg.

formulas.name: Gravity above the surface
formulas.note: Below the surface (uniform Earth): g_d = g(1 − d/R).

formulas.name: Orbital speed
formulas.note: Near the surface v ≈ √(gR) ≈ 7.9 km/s.

formulas.name: Escape speed
formulas.note: Earth ≈ 11.2 km/s; independent of the mass of the object.

formulas.name: Kepler's third law
formulas.note: T² ∝ r³ for bodies orbiting the same central mass.

formulas.name: Gravitational potential energy
formulas.note: Zero at infinity; total energy of an orbit = −GMm/(2r).

formulas.name: Atmospheric and fluid pressure
formulas.note: About 10 m of water exerts 1 atm.

formulas.name: Wien's displacement law
formulas.note: Hotter bodies peak at shorter wavelengths.

formulas.name: Stefan–Boltzmann law
formulas.formula: P = σAT⁴, σ = 5.67 × 10⁻⁸ W m⁻² K⁻⁴
formulas.note: Total power radiated by a black body; multiply by emissivity for real bodies.

formulas.name: Astronomical distances
formulas.note: Light-year and parsec are distances, not times.

formulas.name: Hubble's law
formulas.note: H₀ ≈ 70 km s⁻¹ Mpc⁻¹; 1/H₀ estimates the age of the universe.

shortcuts.name: Escape = √2 × orbital
shortcuts.rule: At the same radius, escape speed is √2 ≈ 1.414 times circular orbital speed.
shortcuts.example: Low Earth orbit 7.9 km/s → escape speed ≈ 7.9 × 1.414 ≈ 11.2 km/s.

shortcuts.name: Kepler scaling
shortcuts.rule: T ∝ r^(3/2): choose radius ratios that are perfect squares.
shortcuts.example: A planet at 4 AU: T = 4^(3/2) = 8 years. At 9 AU: 27 years. Saturn at about 9.5 AU takes about 29 years.

shortcuts.name: Gravity at height R
shortcuts.rule: At height h = R the distance from the centre doubles, so g falls to g/4; inside a uniform Earth g ∝ r.
shortcuts.example: At 6400 km altitude: g ≈ 9.8/4 ≈ 2.45 m/s². Halfway to the centre: g ≈ 4.9 m/s².

shortcuts.name: Wien in one division
shortcuts.rule: λ_max = 2.9 × 10⁻³ / T; about 500 nm for the Sun, about 10 μm for the Earth.
shortcuts.example: Sun 5800 K: 2.9 × 10⁻³/5800 = 5.0 × 10⁻⁷ m = 500 nm (visible). Earth 290 K: 1.0 × 10⁻⁵ m = 10 μm (infrared), which greenhouse gases absorb.

shortcuts.name: T⁴ and light-time
shortcuts.rule: Double the temperature → 16 times the radiated power. Light time = distance ÷ (3 × 10⁸).
shortcuts.example: A star twice as hot with the same size radiates 16 times more. Sun to Earth: 1.5 × 10¹¹/3 × 10⁸ = 500 s ≈ 8.3 min. Moon to Earth: 3.84 × 10⁸/3 × 10⁸ ≈ 1.3 s.

shortcuts.name: Order mnemonics
shortcuts.rule: Planets: My Very Educated Mother Just Served Us Noodles (Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune). Atmosphere upwards: The Strong Man's Tie Exploded (Troposphere, Stratosphere, Mesosphere, Thermosphere, Exosphere).
shortcuts.example: Which layer holds the ozone layer? Second word, Strong → stratosphere. Fourth planet from the Sun? Mother → Mars.

traps: Saying summer happens because the Earth is closer to the Sun; the Earth is actually nearest the Sun in early January.
Calling a light-year a unit of time.
Thinking astronauts in orbit have no gravity acting on them; g at the ISS altitude is still about 90% of surface g.
Placing a geostationary satellite over any latitude; it must be above the equator.
Assuming g keeps increasing as you go down a mine; for a uniform Earth it decreases towards the centre.
nsmqTips: Many questions here are pure recall: layers, planet order, seismic waves, greenhouse gases. Use the mnemonics and answer in one word.
For gravity and orbit ratios, write the proportionality (g ∝ 1/r², T² ∝ r³, P ∝ T⁴) and scale; do not substitute G.
Remember the Earth numbers: R ≈ 6400 km, g ≈ 9.8 m/s², orbital speed 7.9 km/s, escape speed 11.2 km/s.
Riddle clues: 'Kármán line' (100 km), 'Van Allen belts', 'Moho', 'shadow zone', 'red giant', 'redshift'.
